chapters.title: Chapter 1
chapters.html:
Not for the first time since Mydeimos’ arrival, Phainon was annoyed.

Mydei had officially joined the Chrysos Heirs the week before, on a day where the sun felt like it would bake anyone who lingered outside for too long upon the stone streets of Okhema. Phainon had been excited to meet a new face, for it had been more than four years since Hyacine had arrived from the Grove. He vibrated with a restless energy, which only grew stronger as he turned his eyes upon Mydei for the first time.

They found the newcomer in the courtyard, walking beside Aglaea as she gave him a tour of the city. Phainon had convinced Castorice to sneak out with him to catch a glimpse of the new addition to their ranks, and upon finding their target, they swiftly hid behind one of the pillars of the courtyard. Phainon peeked around the pillar, hoping to sneak in a peek without getting caught, but the sight before him caused him to lose his balance as he leaned a bit too far to the side.

The man shone under the hot sun, face turned away from Phainon as he followed Aglaea, his golden hair glinting under the light. He seemed to be practically carved from gold, from his skin to his armor—all except for the tips of his hair, which were dyed a deep crimson, a woven braid hanging along one side of his head. Well muscled and half-dressed, with red markings upon his back and arms, the man could have been mistaken for a mythical hero from times of old.

The scuff of Phainon’s shoes upon the stones betrayed their presence. The newcomer and Aglaea turned to see Phainon and Castorice, neither of whom spoke immediately in hopes of avoiding Aglaea’s knowing stare. The pair was most definitely supposed to be in the Garden of Life at this hour, assisting Hyacine with training the chimeras. Aglaea, uncharacteristically merciful, said nothing, instead motioning to the two of them while addressing the new recruit.

“Mydeimos, this is Castorice and Phainon, two of your fellow Chrysos Heirs,” Aglaea said as she introduced them. “Castorice, Phainon, this is Mydeimos. I’m sure the two of you will make sure Mydeimos settles in well here in Okhema,” she said with a pointed gaze. “Which includes setting a good example, such as not skipping out on your duties.”

Phainon threw a shameless smile onto his face. “Yes, Lady Aglaea. We couldn’t help it, we just wanted to catch a glimpse of our new friend!”

From beside him, Castorice let out a polite cough. “Apologies, Lady Aglaea. I only wanted to make sure Phainon did not manage to cause any trouble.”

Phainon would have shot her a glare, but in the spirit of companionship he turned to Mydeimos instead. “Ah, Mydeimos, it is a pleasure to make your acquaintance. Please let me know if there is anything I can assist you with to make your transition here easier.” He beamed at Mydei eagerly.

However, Mydei only looked at him with a distant glance, and gave him a shallow nod. “Thank you.”

A few beats of silence later, and Phainon realized Mydei was not going to say anything else.

…That’s it?

Clearly, Mydei was a man of few words. Phainon couldn’t help but feel slighted. He had always prided himself on being a friendly face, one people couldn’t help but feel comfortable with right away. Mydei’s silence felt like a blow to his pride.

He shook the feeling off. No matter. He would break the ice somehow.

Aglaea sent him and Castorice back to the Garden shortly after, but Phainon’s excitement at Mydei’s arrival still burned under his skin, lasting until dinner time, when Mydei finally joined the whole group for dinner.

Unfortunately, that excitement dimmed very quickly, when Phainon realized that Mydeimos was not going to be goaded into socializing that easily.

Mydeimos sat in the middle of the Chrysos Heirs, but did not join the conversation unless he was asked a question directly, and even then he would respond with brief, cursory answers, usually not even exceeding a few words.

Phainon returned home feeling more irritated than he had in a long time. He knew that he wasn’t entitled to Mydei’s friendship, but Mydei’s unwillingness to make even simple conversation made Phainon feel like working alongside him would be fraught with tension— and as a team, tension was the last thing they needed. The task of making people feel comfortable usually fell to Phainon, but never before had he encountered a person as reticent as Mydei.

For the sake of the team, for the sake of Okhema—Phainon had to break Mydei’s shell wide open.

Unfortunately, a week passed and Phainon was no closer to accomplishing his goal.

He had tried sitting next to Mydei at meals, but Mydei was no more forthcoming than he had been on his arrival. He never ignored Phainon, nor failed to answer his admittedly incessant questions, but his answers were never more than two or three words, and by the end of the third day, Phainon was no closer to understanding Mydei than before.

The first week passed by at a snail’s pace, and Phainon felt like he had made no progress in integrating Mydei into the Chrysos Heirs. The itch of frustration nagged at him, but Phainon could do nothing about it. He said as much to Castorice one night over drinks in the market.

“I just can’t understand him, Cas. Like, what do I even do?” Phainon took another swig from his second bottle, his words already slurring.

Castorice sighed loudly. “Phainon, you can’t force the man to be friends with you.” Her face was slightly flushed, but Phainon knew that was practically as red as Castorice ever got. They usually went out for drinks every weekend, to drain off some of the stress from their busy schedules during the week. Phainon enjoyed the routine of it, even if it technically counted as an excess expense. He didn’t like spending his hard-earned money on frivolous things, but these weekly outings felt necessary to retain some of his sanity.

Phainon echoed her sigh. “I know, I know. But… People usually like me. Why doesn’t he like me?” he whined.

“Is that what this is about? Really, Phainon?” Castorice asked with a snort.

“No! Yes. Kinda?” Phainon’s thoughts jumbled in his head. “I mean, yes, I want to be his friend. But mostly I want us all to get along. It’s been so long since we’ve had someone new join the Flame Chase, Cas…” Phainon sighed again, already sounding like a broken record even to himself. “Everyone else gets along, so why can’t he?” he asked mournfully.

“Maybe he just prefers to be alone. And that’s okay, Phainon. Plus,” she added with a pointed look, “Mydei isn’t everyone. Haven’t you seen him fight yet?”

Phainon hadn’t. He shook his head.

Castorice widened her eyes, jabbing a finger at his forehead. “Go watch him train tomorrow. Then you’ll see.”

Phainon didn’t know what good that would do, but he had to admit he was curious. “Fine,” he grumbled. Mydei had been recruited to the Flame-Chase for a reason, and it certainly wasn’t due to his sparkling wit. Time for Phainon to see what he was really working with.

The next morning, Phainon dragged himself out of bed, splashed some water on his face and headed to the training arena after a quick breakfast. Castorice told him that Mydei usually trained before their morning duties began, before Entry Hour had fully given way to the light of the day.

Yawning, Phainon rubbed his face as he neared the training grounds. It was quiet, but he could just make out the sounds of the shifting of dirt, sandals scuffing the earth. He rounded the corner of the arena wall and stopped in his tracks.

Mydeimos was indeed there. That wasn’t what had surprised Phainon. It was just… Phainon hadn’t known what to expect, but he hadn’t imagined Mydei’s movements would be so...beautiful.

Mydei moved swiftly as he trained, each movement quick and precise, each position held with grace and no sign of discomfort. Phainon could see the strength behind each strike, the sword in his hand never wavering. He wasn’t sure how long he stood at the entrance, staring, but he watched Mydei until the sun had risen fully and his neck began to sweat, stirring him out of his stupor.

Mydei finally stopped and returned his sword to the weapon rack. Phainon stood up a bit straighter as Mydei faced him, crossing his arms upon his chest.

He had surely seen Phainon watching him, but had not commented on his feelings on the matter. Instead he stood there, gaze meeting Phainon’s. Phainon was startled to realize that Mydei was waiting for his evaluation.

“I was not aware you were so talented with a sword, Mydeimos,” Phainon called out cheerfully.

Mydei dipped his head in a nod. “I usually prefer to fight with my hands, but I wanted to try something new,” he responded.

Phainon stared. Something new? Something new? The words spun around and around in his head as he tried to process what he had just heard.

In an instant, all his years of learned politeness and etiquette went out the window, and Phainon could not have controlled the words that came out of his mouth next if he had tried.

“Will you fight me?”

Mydei stared at him.

Phainon’s words burst out of him, unrestrained. “It’s just—I’ve never seen someone fight so beautifully, and that’s not even your weapon of choice? I want to see you fight for real.”

“No,” Mydei said.

Phainon could only gape at him. “But… Why not?”

“I do not want to fight you,” Mydei said.

Phainon had no reply. He could only watch as Mydei left the arena, brushing past silently as he stood rooted in his place. While watching Mydei train, all of the frustrations of the past week had all disappeared, leaving only awe of Mydei’s talent in its place. Now, those feelings swept back and hit Phainon like a raging force, giving him whiplash. Phainon was, once again, incredibly annoyed.

What was he supposed to do in the face of such stubbornness?

chapters.title: Chapter 2
chapters.html:
Phainon had many good traits, but knowing when to give up was unfortunately not one of them. After seeing Mydei train, Phainon made it his mission to make Mydei give in. He would somehow make Mydei fight with him, whatever it took.

Whatever it took, he had thought. That was how he had landed in his current situation.

Phainon stood in front of Aglaea in the Hero’s Bath, sopping wet and hair mussed, dripping onto the carefully polished tiles. Aglaea considered him for several long moments, then finally spoke.

“Are you quite in possession of all your faculties, Phainon?”

Phainon winced. Aglaea would not be pulling her punches today. He nodded.

“Then, are you perhaps ill? Injured?”

He shook his head.

Aglaea’s stare pierced through him. “Then what could possibly be the cause of such unruly behavior?”

Phainon held his tongue. He had no good answer to why Aglaea had found him facedown in the public baths, the heat of the water so high that it had made him nearly drown the baths in his sweat. He had challenged Mydei to a test of endurance, to see who could last longest in the sweltering heat.

Mydei hadn’t said anything, only closing his eyes as he sat down in the clear water. Phainon had lasted for nearly two quints, only getting up to follow Mydei as he made to leave, but Phainon had overestimated his stamina and passed out right there onto the gleaming tiles. It was a miracle of the Titans he hadn’t cracked his head where he fell.

Phainon hung his head low in shame. He hadn’t meant to make a fool of himself like that. And, as much as he disliked it, the incident had also brought shame upon the Chrysos Heirs —for one of Okhema’s strongest protectors to keel over in the public baths, surely the members of the Flame-Chase must not be as indomitable as Aglaea proclaimed.

He could feel Aglaea’s gaze lingering, but he still said nothing. He had gotten far too ahead of himself, only thinking of his own selfish needs, and had disgraced himself and his companions.

“Phainon,” Aglaea said, voice gentler.

He looked back up at her. Aglaea no longer looked like he wanted to skewer him. Instead, her eyes were softer now as she gazed at him.

“I just—” he finally spoke, his voice dry. He started again. “I just…want Mydei to feel welcome here.”

Aglaea considered him for a moment, and then nodded. “I understand, Phainon.” She walked around her desk to sit down, and motioned for him to do the same.

“Mydeimos is…a special case. He has immense strength, and a soul of great value, but he has also known more pain than most,” Aglaea said.

“I do not think he wishes this to be widely known, but he is the crown prince of Castrum Kremnos.”

Phainon’s heart thudded dully in his chest. Crown prince.

The story of Castrum Kremnos was known to all in Okhema. Once a shining city of crimson and gold, it had been the very pinnacle of military might and heroic valor, now reduced to crumbling ruins. The dynasty had fallen after King Eurypon’s death by the hand of his son ten years ago, its people scattered to the wind as the city was invaded by the black tide.

Now, Castrum Kremnos was a name only spoken of in hushed whispers, the plight of its remaining descendants unknown and left to rot.

“He has wandered for a long time, and has experienced many sorrows since Kremnos’s fall. I do not believe, Phainon, that he will ever fully feel welcome here, or anywhere, for that matter.” Aglaea’s words were chosen with care, her face impassive save for a slight shadow in her eyes.

Phainon couldn’t reply. His throat felt tight. It all made sense now. Mydei’s fighting prowess, the elegance in the way he moved, like nothing Phainon had ever seen—relics of a time long past, belonging to a lineage that no longer existed.

Mydeimos had to be so lonely.

Not only after losing his kingdom, having to kill his mad father, but—Phainon suddenly recalled something he had heard when he was a boy, from a story about the crown prince of Castrum Kremnos.

“Is he…truly immortal?” Phainon asked slowly.

Aglaea nodded. “Yes, immortal of mind and body. Some call it a blessing, others a curse… But I suppose for the son of Strife, it is also an unshakeable duty.”

The duty of defending Amphoreus from the black tide, from the monsters that threatened the edges of the world, could only ever belong to the descendants of Strife.

Phainon felt sick.

“I know you wish to help him settle in, Phainon. But it may be that he will never find a place of his own again. That depends solely on Mydeimos himself.”

Aglaea’s words echoed through his head as he trudged home. He had thought that Mydei just needed a little time to adjust, and that no matter how quiet he seemed, he would eventually see Okhema as a safe place, and the Chrysos Heirs would make him feel welcomed, and they would all get along. Another gleaming cog in the well-oiled machine of Okhema’s strongest.

Phainon knew he could be a little short sighted on occasion, but never before had he felt so naive. Mydeimos was never going to be just another Chrysos Heir—his fighting prowess made that extremely clear. Mydeimos clearly had reason to not want to make friends, and even if Phainon wanted to understand him more, knock down the impenetrable wall of steel Mydei had placed between them, it was not Phainon’s decision.

It never had been.

Phainon’s head ached, and he threw himself atop his bed with a muffled hmph and closed his eyes. He dreamed of marble halls, rivers of crimson running into the sea, golden hair sinking like a stone, fading into black.

After hearing the truth of who Mydei really was, Phainon left the Kremnoan alone. He no longer had the urge to push Mydei’s boundaries, not after catching a glimpse of what truly lay behind his reticence. Mydei had lost his home, his family, everything.

Phainon knew what that was like. He did not want to intrude on Mydei’s life any longer.

The shift in Phainon’s behavior was evident. He did not follow Mydei around like a lost puppy anymore, nor beg him to fight with him at the arena after watching Mydei train. Phainon returned to spending his lunches with Castorice, which earned him several curious looks.

“Did something happen?”

Phainon looked up from his plate, mouth still half-full of food.

He hastily swallowed. “No.”

Castorice gave him a knowing look. “You’ve spent the last two weeks bothering Mydei, and now you’re back here? Phainon, I’m not stupid.”

Phainon shoveled the rest of the food in his mouth. “I mean it. Nothing happened,” he said as he stood up to return his plate.

Castorice didn’t say anything more as he walked away, but Phainon felt her violet gaze upon his shoulder blades until he left the canteen.

He didn’t know how to explain his recent behavior. Mydei’s secret wasn’t Phainon’s to tell, and as much as he wanted to share his recent turmoil, he felt bound by responsibility, and so could not tell Castorice. Let everyone think he’d lost interest in annoying Mydei, and that he’d moved on. It’s not like he could tell them anything different.

In the meantime, Phainon threw himself into his duties. Technically, the Chrysos Heirs were tasked with protecting Okhema from hostile threats, which sometimes meant going out on missions to fight the black tide, or capturing people who had committed crimes in the city to be punished. Most days, however, were extremely boring, with the duty of patrolling the city and the outlying areas split amongst the Chrysos Heirs, meaning Phainon really only patrolled once a week. Other than that, most of his time was spent in the Garden of Life helping Hyacine, or assisting to maintain the baths or the stables, or even mediating conflicts between citizens.

Most people assumed the Flame-Chase took most of the Chrysos Heirs’ time and energy, but in periods such as these, when there was not so much as a whiff of a Coreflame within reach, the Heirs only had weekly meetings to discuss the Flame-Chase.

So Phainon was lucky enough to have lots of menial labor to keep his mind off of the crown prince of Castrum Kremnos.

It worked for a while, with Phainon avoiding any thought of the golden-haired man until the day he was finally assigned to patrol alongside Mydei.

Their shift started at the top of Parting Hour, when the sun began to turn everything its rays touched into soft gold. After dinner, Phainon stood outside of Marmoreal Palace to wait.

Mydei arrived not long after Phainon, armor glinting in the evening sun. It had been nearly three weeks since the baths, and Phainon hadn’t spoken more than a few words to him in that time.

Mydei looked at him from the bottom of the steps, and said, “Let’s go.”

Phainon nodded, and pushed away from the wall he had been leaning against. “All right.”

The patrol was quiet. Neither of them spoke. Phainon felt his skin begin to itch with the need to fill the silence, but he clamped the words down, the only sound at this hour being the rasp of their sandals on the stones.

It wasn’t until night had fallen and they returned to the steps of Marmoreal Palace that Mydei broke the silence.

“You…” he began.

Phainon stopped, turning around to face Mydei where he stood a few steps below him. “Yes?” he asked quizzically.

Mydei stared at him impassively. “I did not take you for a quiet man.”

Phainon blinked. When he didn’t answer right away, Mydei continued. “Have I done something wrong?”

Phainon couldn’t speak for a moment, but then shook his head. “No, no, I just… I’ve had some things on my mind.”

Mydei was still looking at him, the sharp glint of his eyes barely visible in the darkness.

Phainon felt an urge to end the conversation quickly, so he scrambled to find an excuse. “I— um, I just… I. Uh. Family stuff. I’m gonna—”

“Lady Aglaea told you.”

Phainon stopped mid-sentence, breath catching in his throat.

“What,”  was all he could manage.

Mydeimos crossed his arms in front of his chest, a familiar sight. “She told me what you discussed that day in the baths,” he said, not sounding particularly angry or surprised.

Phainon didn’t know how to respond. “Yeah. Uh, she did.”

Mydei didn’t say anything, so Phainon gathered his words and asked, cautiously. “You… aren’t angry?”

“No,” Mydei replied. “It is who I am. Just because I did not say it does not mean I am ashamed of it.”

“I didn’t—”

“But you pity me,” Mydei’s words cut in.

Phainon stared at him. Mydei thought Phainon pitied him? He realized that he hadn’t disputed the accusation quickly enough only when Mydei’s gaze shuttered and his mouth drew back into a hard line.

“I do not need your pity, Deliverer.”

“I never said—”

“Enough,” Mydei spat. “I am not deserving of your pity, so save it. I do not wish to gain the approval of this city by making Okhemans cry as they listen to my story of woe and anguish.”

With not even so much as a glance in acknowledgement, Mydei spun on his heel and stalked away. Phainon’s blood boiled under his skin, anger pulsing in his chest.

Mydei thought Phainon pitied him, and hadn’t let Phainon speak more than two words in his defense. His body felt full of liquid fire, and Phainon couldn’t bear to watch Mydei’s form retreat in the distance, so Phainon left in the direction of his apartment, anger still simmering under his veins.

Phainon could deal with a lot of attacks against his character, but could not deal with the fact that Mydei thought he was so low as to pity him. Once he could think straight without wanting to yell, Phainon would have to make that clear, one way or another.

chapters.html:
Phainon rarely ever was really, truly angry. This, however, was one of those times.

Mydei thought Phainon pitied him, which couldn’t have been farther from the truth. How could Phainon pity him, when Phainon himself had been through similar pain?

Pity was born of condescension, was shallow and distant. What Phainon felt was something sharp and very, very close to home. If he had to choose one word to describe the mix of emotions he was feeling, Phainon thought it would probably be…empathy.

Pity was feeling sorry for someone, showing compassion for someone who had gone through something, but pity only required seeing the negative effects the something had brought. Empathy, however, meant that you felt the effects of the something too. Phainon had gone through many somethings, and no matter how different his situation was to Mydei’s, the fact of the matter was that Phainon knew how Mydei felt.

And so it hurt Phainon, more than his pride would allow, to have Mydei believe Phainon pitied him.

It took Phainon a very long time to reach sleep that night, and he woke up feeling tense and off-kilter. He stumbled through his morning routine, and somehow managed to make it through his morning duties without tripping over his feet.

”Snowy!” a sweet voice chirped from behind him as he made his way to the Garden of Life in search of Mydei, after failing to find him elsewhere. Phainon turned and saw Tribbie, a basket of chimera treats in her arms as she bounded towards him.

“Lady Tribbie!” Phainon greeted her with a smile, his poor mood somewhat discarded at the sight of her.

“Snowy… Did you stay up too late again?” Tribbie frowned up at him, her red hair bouncing as she bobbed on her tiptoes, trying to examine his face more closely.

“Couldn’t sleep,” Phainon said sheepishly.

Tribbie somehow frowned harder. “Too much excitement late in the day will do that, you know! It’s like you’re still a little kid, Phainon,” she chastised.

Phainon fought the urge to roll his eyes, which he knew would earn him a light smack on his arm. Changing the subject, he asked brightly, “Are you off to the Garden, then? I’ll gladly take those to Miss Hyacine for you!”

“No, no, I can do it myself! Besides, I’ve got to talk to Cinny anyway,” Tribbie said with a giggle, already setting off in the direction of the Garden.

When they arrived, the Garden was alight with activity. Apparently, Hyacine was preparing to host an event, the details eluding Phainon as he made his way through the throngs of workers carrying supplies to and fro.

Amidst the hubbub, Phainon saw Mydei not far from where he was walking with Tribbie. Phainon excused himself and walked up to him, not wanting to miss this opportunity.

“Mydeimos,” Phainon said.

Mydei turned, seeing him for the first time. “Deliverer,” Mydei responded in lieu of greeting, a thread of tension present in his golden eyes.

Deliverer. Besides Aglaea, Mydei was the only one who had ever called Phainon that. But now was not the time to ask about it.

“Can we talk?” Phainon asked, aware that this was the most courteous that he had ever been to Mydei. That was, of course, because before Phainon had never actually asked Mydei if he wanted to talk, only taking Mydei's silence as an excuse to press forward.

Mydei cast him a level look. After a moment Mydei nodded, apparently seeing something in Phainon’s gaze that made him acquiesce.

They went to one of the corridors encircling the Garden, searching for one that was unoccupied and found an alcove where they could speak freely.

For a moment, it was silent. Phainon knew he needed to be the one who spoke first but took a few extra moments to gather his courage.

”I do not pity you,” Phainon began quietly. Mydei said nothing, only listened as if he knew Phainon had more to say.

“Have you ever heard of Aedes Elysiae?”

Mydei shook his head.

“That was where I grew up.” Phainon shifted his gaze to watch the shadows flicker on the wall across from them. “It was surrounded by wheat fields, as far as the eye could see. The sea was right there, too. I used to sit on the dock for hours, staring at where the sunlight met the water. I think I might have permanently damaged my vision doing that,” Phainon winced, remembering.

“The air smelled sweet, of wheat and flowers, and—” Phainon’s head hurt a little, but he continued—“there were fairies, I think. Though I might have made that up. In any case, I had a happy childhood, running through the fields, playing hide and seek with the, um, fairies and my friend—Cyrene.” Phainon didn’t want to say her name but forced himself to anyway, ignoring the pang it brought.

Mydei hadn’t moved or said a word, so Phainon took it as permission and pressed on.

“But, the black tide eventually came. We were such a small village, with no way of knowing it was coming, with no neighbors to lend us their aid. It’s…um, it’s all ash now.” Phainon forced the words out. “I—anyway, I was the only one who ended up making it to Okhema. I was fourteen. Once they found out I bled golden blood, Aglaea brought me here.”

Phainon’s words kept falling out of his mouth, the shudder in his breath nearly betraying him. He was almost done.

”Ever since then, I have worked so, so hard to integrate myself into this city, with these people. I studied debate, learned etiquette and practiced the most I ever have, so that one day, I might not feel as out of place here. And yet,” Phainon looked back over at Mydei, “I still feel so alone.”

Mydei was still listening.

“So,” Phainon said. “I do not pity you, Mydeimos.”

Phainon hoped that was enough. He did not have the strength to express all of the emotions that swirled around in his heart at the moment, and hoped that Mydei would understand what he was trying to say. His heart pounded thickly, uncomfortable in the silence of the empty corridor.

There was nothing for a few moments more, until Mydei finally responded.

”Good,” Mydeimos said.

With that, the Kremnoan left. Phainon watched his retreating form until Mydei turned the corner, heading back in the direction of the Garden.

Phainon had no clue what Mydei was thinking, but nonetheless couldn’t help but feel the tiniest bit comforted.

After that, Mydei’s behavior towards Phainon decidedly changed. He would greet Phainon in passing, and respond to questions in longer sentences than before. They weren’t long by any means, or detailed, but it was such a marked shift from the past few months that Phainon couldn’t help but be taken aback.

Most notably, however, was that Mydei began sitting with Phainon during meals.

Phainon still hadn’t told Castorice about Mydei, or about their conversation outside the Garden, but Castorice seemed to know he had a good reason for not bringing it up, and had mercifully avoided the subject since that first day.

Presently, they were arguing about the recent increase of Aglaea’s parchment purchases. Phainon thought he might have finally convinced Castorice of his hypothesis when she suddenly stopped, but realized that she had only paused to acknowledge someone behind him.

“Good afternoon, Mydei,” she said politely.

Phainon’s eyes widened and he went to turn around in his seat, but it ended up being in vain, as Mydei sat down beside Phainon with his cup and plate of food.

“Good afternoon, Castorice,” Mydei said.

Phainon stared at him. Mydei only acknowledged him with a glance and then began to eat.

…This was new. The Chrysos Heirs ate lunch together every day, but Mydei had always eaten at his own table, never joining one of the various groups that were spread throughout the canteen.

Phainon didn’t really know what to do with this new development, but supposed he couldn’t complain. So he turned back to Castorice, continuing their conversation where they had left off.

“I’m telling you, Aglaea’s been writing letters like crazy.”

“That doesn’t mean she’s courting someone!”

“Why else would she be sending letters twice a week? And to the Grove, no less,” Phainon said, shooting Castorice a knowing look over his sandwich.

“Oh, I don’t know, Phainon, maybe she’s just doing her job?”

Phainon threw his hands up in the air. “That’s a flimsy excuse, and you know it.”

“She could have found a pen pal.”

“Who sends letters twice a week to a mere pen pal?” Mydei’s voice came from beside Phainon.

The two of them looked over at Mydei, surprised. Mydei looked a bit as if he did not mean to say that out loud, but did not back down, golden eyes shimmering with the tiniest hint of mirth.

Phainon was the first to recover. “You see? Even Mydeimos agrees with me. I knew I wasn’t imagining things.”

Castorice only let out a small huff of defeat and changed the subject, clearly not wanting to linger on a losing battle now that she was outnumbered.

After that, Mydei’s presence beside Phainon became a part of his new normal. Phainon figured that after their talk the other day, Mydei seemed to…accept him. Or at least, not resent his presence. It warmed Phainon’s heart more than he wanted to admit that Phainon was the one Mydei had chosen to grace his presence with. Mydei did also start interacting more with Castorice as well, but that was honestly only because she and Phainon were mostly always together.

Mydei may not want to make friends, per se, but he had at least accepted Phainon’s presence in his life. That was not an insignificant development in the least.

Chapter End Notes

After that, the ice between Mydei and Phainon finally broke, giving way to a quiet acquaintanceship. Phainon didn’t delude himself into thinking they had magically become friends, but at least Mydei wasn’t holding him at arm’s length anymore. Phainon could be content with that.

At least, he thought he could.

Standing once again in the practice arena one morning a few days later, watching Mydei’s flawless form move effortlessly as he trained, Phainon’s mouth went dry.

As hard as he tried to control himself, he still really, really, really wanted to spar with Mydei.

After Mydei finished, he walked over to where Phainon was waiting so they could leave for midday patrol together.

“What,” Mydei asked.

“Huh?” Phainon shook himself out of his daze.

“You’re looking at me weirdly,” Mydei said, golden eyes narrowed.

“I was just thinking how I really do want to fight you,” said Phainon.

“No.”

“Why not?”

Mydei glared at him. “Because I said no.” He started walking, not bothering to wait for Phainon.

“Why, afraid you’ll hurt me, Mydeimos?” Phainon jogged to catch up to him, slowing when he reached Mydei’s side.

Mydei didn’t respond.

”Or is it that I’m not worthy of fighting the crown prince of Castrum Kremnos?” Phainon teased, seeing no one around to eavesdrop.

Mydei glanced over at him but did not refute it.

Phainon’s jaw dropped. “Well, that is just mean, Mydeimos. I’ll have you know that I am the strongest fighter in Okhema! I can definitely handle whatever you throw at me.”

Mydei did not dignify that with a response.

Unfortunately, Mydei had the incredible luck of being stuck with Phainon for the time being, and Phainon did not relent in his pursuit of a spar for the entire patrol.

By the time they returned, Mydei looked like he wanted to shove Phainon into the nearest fountain, but did not so much as even try to lift a finger in his direction, much to Phainon’s chagrin.

Phainon knew he was pushing Mydei’s boundaries again, but the fact that Mydei continued to stick around him made Phainon think that Mydei didn’t really mind all that much. After all, Mydei could just go back to eating on his own if Phainon truly annoyed him, but every day at lunchtime, Mydei sat next to Phainon without fail.

So, Phainon reasoned, if Mydei needed someone to blame for Phainon’s pestering, he could really only blame himself.

The days flew by in a comfortable manner, with Phainon continuing to bother Mydei to no avail.

Eventually, the month of Freedom gave way to the month of Reaping, marking the start of preparations for the Festival of Cerces. The festival celebrated the beginning of the harvest season, which to most people meant a time of celebration and praise, but to Phainon meant that a sharp ache came to awareness in his chest, one that he could not shake away until the weather cooled and the leaves had all fallen from the trees.

Harvest time brought back too many painful memories, so Phainon naturally avoided anything to do with the Festival of Cerces. At least, he tried to. As part of the city leadership in Okhema, the Chrysos Heirs were tasked with the preparation and execution of the important festivals during the year, the harvest festival being one of the largest.

Every year, Phainon resigned himself to keep busy and his mind far away from useless thoughts. But every year he failed, the tightness in his chest giving way to sleepless nights and deep bags underneath his eyes. Phainon knew no matter what he did, this month would pass the same as it did every year.

Castorice knew better than to comment on it, as did most of the other Chrysos Heirs. Only Castorice knew the reason behind Phainon’s shift in mood, but even she did not know the details. Even so, she never pressed, only giving Phainon a quiet nod when he told her that he wouldn’t be available for drinks that week.

Instead, he went to the training arena after dinner. By this hour it would be empty, and Phainon could not be around another person for a moment longer. Nor could he go home and sleep, for he would only toss and turn until dawn. And even if he could sleep, Phainon knew nothing pleasant would appear in his dreams.

So, he trained. The arena had gone dark, the only sounds being the swish of Phainon’s clothing as he moved through his forms and the shuffling of the dirt underneath his feet.

He didn’t know how long he practiced for, only that when he stopped his muscles were burning and his heart pounding, the sound echoing through his head. He shut his eyes as he caught his breath, breathing in the cool night air, his greatsword landing in the dirt.

Phainon had only closed his eyes for a moment when his vision turned orange, lungs full of the scratchiness of smoke. His heartbeat sounded too loud for his chest, and Phainon felt a familiar sense of dread seize his bones.

Fuck. Fuck, not now.

Phainon’s eyes burst open, and he made to leave, except—Mydei was standing in the entrance, watching him.

Seeing Phainon had noticed him, Mydei spoke.

“Do you always train in the dark?”

Phainon could not respond. He needed to leave.

He grabbed his greatsword from the dirt, but as he tried to walk past Mydei, he found his arm caught in the other’s grasp.

Before Mydei could speak, Phainon wrenched his arm back. He couldn’t do this right now. His breaths were already getting shorter. He couldn’t be here.

Again Phainon tried to leave, but the shapeless emotions he had been fighting finally caught up with him, striking him all at once, causing him to stumble. The strength of the emotions almost forced him to his knees as he gasped for breath.

The pain in his chest made it hard to think, or breathe, or see. Phainon stopped existing for a moment, the ache in his chest almost strangling him. All he felt was that all-consuming fear, and he was back in Aedes Elysiae, watching everyone he knew die before him. He couldn’t think, couldn’t remember anything except for those scorched memories, and he burned. He was too slow, too weak, too far away to help.

Fire, smoke, screaming. Phainon couldn’t breathe.

All of a sudden he was aware of a certain pressure on his body. Through the dizzying swirl of panic Phainon was fighting he slowly became aware of something encircling his arm, a molten pressure.

It grounded Phainon for a second, and for a moment he could hear again.

“Breathe, just take a breath. There you go. You’re okay. Just breathe, Deliverer.”

Through his daze, Phainon vaguely recognized Mydeimos’ voice. Right. Mydei was there. Phainon struggled to control his breathing, and after an indeterminable amount of time, the crushing weight on his chest lessened, and his vision cleared.

Phainon belatedly realized that he was now sitting down, leaned against one of the benches encircling the training arena. Mydei sat close beside him, concern visible in his sharp eyes.

“Mydeimos,” Phainon said. Or tried to. It ended up sounding more like a croak.

“Just keep breathing,” said Mydei.

Phainon put his head in his hands and kept breathing. He tried to feel anything but shame, to paste on the easygoing expression he usually bore so lightly, but could not muster the strength.

After a while, he could not stand it anymore. Phainon stood, brushing off the dirt where it clung to his white clothes.

Mydei stood with him, but did not say anything yet.

Phainon tried to smile, but it felt brittle. “Thanks,” he said, voice still sounding more fragile than he wanted it to.

“Do you…want to talk about it?” Mydei asked quietly.

Phainon thought for a moment. “No,” he answered, voice cracking. “I just want to stop thinking about it.”

Mydeimos considered him. “All right.”

Phainon took that as his cue to leave, but no sooner had he turned away did Mydei’s voice echo from behind.

“Then… Do you still want to fight me?”

“Then… Do you still want to fight me?”

At those words, Phainon stopped. His head still hurt, the aching in his chest still pulsing under his skin, but Mydei’s offer cut through Phainon’s muddled thoughts like a knife.

“I thought you said no,” said Phainon, confused.

Mydei was still looking straight at Phainon, hiding nothing.

“My pride will survive,” he replied.

Something in Phainon’s heart twisted. “Are you doing this because you feel sorry for me?”

“No,” Mydei said. “I am doing this because I have stood where you stand now.”

Phainon looked at Mydei for a few moments longer, assessing.

“All right,” said Phainon finally.

At Phainon’s words, Mydei went to the weapon rack and picked up the sword he often practiced with, adjusting his grip until it felt comfortable. Then he faced Phainon, waiting for his advance.

Phainon’s greatsword was still on the ground where he had dropped it, so Phainon retrieved it and readied his stance. Then, he moved.

Mydei met his strike with a clang. Phainon had the advantage since his sword was larger and heavier, but the force behind Mydei’s parry was stronger than Phainon had anticipated, causing Phainon’s weight to list unexpectedly. Mydei took advantage of Phainon’s shift in balance and counterattacked, blade moving swiftly to jab at Phainon’s exposed stomach.

Phainon managed to dodge just in time, but it was a near thing. Chest heaving, Phainon studied Mydei.

Oh, this was going to be fun.

The two of them fought furiously, the sound of steel meeting steel echoing through the chilly darkness. With every strike, Phainon’s thoughts traitorously threatened to rise up to choke him again, but he fought them back, trying to focus on the rhythm of Mydei’s movements, on meeting the slash of his blade.

“Focus,” Mydei growled.

Phainon gritted his teeth and parried the incoming strike with an oomph, almost losing his balance, but his mind returned to the fight before him.

Phainon wasn’t sure how long the fight lasted, but after a long period both of them just stood there, breathing heavily, their bodies mutually deciding to call a truce.

“You fought well,” said Mydei, hair damp with sweat.

Phainon acknowledged that with a nod. “...Thank you.”

A trickle of golden blood dripped from Phainon’s brow, and he wiped it away with a grimace. Mydei’s blade had broken his skin several times, all of them only shallow cuts, though there were too many for Phainon’s comfort. Phainon had only managed to nick Mydei twice, but both times the cuts had closed up within seconds, leaving only slight shimmers of gold to indicate that Phainon’s blade had ever met its target.

It both frustrated and fascinated Phainon, and he was once again reminded of the marvel that was Mydei’s immortal body. Phainon was suddenly struck by a thought he’d never had before.

“Say, Mydeimos,” he began. “Has no one else realized your body heals itself?”

Someone had to have noticed. Mydei’s status as the immortal crown prince of Castrum Kremnos was not widely known, even to the Chrysos Heirs, but surely Mydei had been hurt in front of someone since arriving in Okhema. Even something as small as a papercut could have given him away.

Mydei walked past him to sit on one of the nearby stone benches, setting his sword down beside him. “No,” he replied. “I am not around anyone long enough for them to notice.”

Phainon didn’t know what to say to that. He went to sit next to Mydei, arms propped behind him to keep his tired body upright.

“Sounds lonely,” Phainon decided.

Mydei sighed, a novel sound. “Perhaps.”

“If…I might be so rude as to ask, would you ever tell the others? About who you are, I mean,” Phainon clarified, gesturing at Mydei’s sitting form with one hand.

Mydei glanced at him. “Who I was, you mean. And what good would it do?” Mydei’s gaze shifted upwards, toward the night sky littered with stars. “I have no claim to that heritage any longer. All I have now is a body that does not perish.”

Phainon considered. “Surely there must be others from Castrum Kremnos who still wish to reunite with their own people. Is that not also a part of you?”

Mydei, somewhat surprisingly, did not bristle at the question, only answered honestly. “Maybe, but they believe the dynasty of Kremnos has not passed on. They would see me as living proof that the glory of Strife still lives. But they are wrong. That legacy died with my father, ten years ago.”

Mydeimos did not sound sad, only regretful as he gazed up at the stars. Phainon felt he was seeing a side of Mydei the other never got to show to anyone—the side that was just a man and not a prince.

After a while, Phainon realized his mouth no longer tasted like ash, and his heartbeat felt far steadier than before. He could still feel the threads of panic where they wrapped around his bones, but they felt thinner and easier to ignore, no longer strangling him from the inside.

Phainon didn’t expect Mydei’s presence to bring him such comfort, but had no intention of complaining. They sat together under the stars, not talking of anything in particular, until Phainon’s eyes finally began to droop and he left in the direction of his apartment.

He didn’t realize how much calmer he felt until the next morning, when Phainon realized he hadn’t dreamed of anything at all.

In exchange for skipping drinks, Phainon had agreed to meet Castorice for breakfast the next day. There was a stall in Marmoreal Market that sold the best honeycakes in Okhema, and the pair had to get there early if they wanted to grab some before they sold out. There seemed to always be a line wrapping around the stall, which only grew longer as the sun ascended into the sky.

As Phainon approached the stall, he saw Castorice had already ordered for both of them. She waved in greeting, but then peered at his face curiously. “Did you get in a fight?”

Phainon was startled for a moment until he realized the cuts on his face must still be visible. “Yeah,” he said, somewhat embarrassed. “I, um, sparred with Mydeimos last night.”

Castorice’s eyes nearly bugged out of her head. “You—with Mydei? Titans, Phainon, tell me everything. You’ve been begging him for months!”

Phainon told her over breakfast. She looked worried to hear that he’d had another episode, but said nothing until he finished narrating the events of last night. Phainon told her as much as he could without spilling Mydei’s secret, but Castorice didn’t push it, even though he could see she knew he wasn’t being entirely forthcoming.

“I’m a bit surprised, to be honest,” Castorice said, swallowing her last bit of hibiscus tea. “I thought he’d get tired of you bugging him to spar all the time.”

Phainon had the good sense to be offended. “I do not bug him,” he said, lying through his teeth. “If he didn’t like it, he would say so.”

Castorice shot him a doubtful look. “Are we talking about the same person?”

Phainon scoffed, shoving a bite of honeycake into his mouth. “Just because he doesn’t talk much doesn’t mean he won’t,” he mumbled around his food. “You know, I even think we’re becoming friends.”

Phainon did, actually. Just a few days before he would have thought it improbable, but after last night, Phainon suddenly didn’t feel friendship with Mydei was completely out of reach. Maybe just a little harder to get to, that’s all.

Now that he’d finally gotten to fight Mydei personally, Phainon couldn’t wait to do it again. Mydei moved like he was dancing, every step fluid and purposeful. Phainon itched to see it again, needed to learn how Mydei did it. He doubted his own way of fighting would ever become as beautiful as Mydei’s, but he’d be damned if he didn’t try.

He hoped Mydei didn’t think Phainon would let their spar be a one-time thing. Because now that the dam had broken, there was no stopping the waters from overtaking everything in their path.

“You know,” Phainon mused one day. “I’ve always wanted to learn Kremnoan.”

Mydei was walking slightly ahead of Phainon, but did not turn his head to face him. “If you think I’m going to be the one to teach you, think again.”

They were outside of Okhema’s walls today, on a mission for Aglaea. There had been an increase in Titankin coming too close to the outlying villages, and the two of them were tasked with cutting down their numbers. Phainon had yet to spot one, but they’d only been outside the city gates for no more than a quint, so Phainon didn’t let his guard down just yet.

“Why not? When else will I have the chance to learn Kremnoan nowadays?” Phainon looked over at Mydei, an innocent expression on his face.

“If you never even encounter the language, why would you want to learn it?” Mydei did turn to face Phainon this time, looking like he was already regretting asking.

Phainon grinned cheekily. “To learn more about you, of course! Plus, there’s some books in Kremnoan in the library that I wanna read.”

“If you can’t even read the titles, why would you want to read them?” Mydei was scowling.

Phainon laughed. “Why, because I like the covers, dear Mydeimos!” He was mostly joking about asking Mydei to teach him, but Phainon had to admit that he was at least a little bit interested. He’d always been drawn to languages, thinking them to be somewhat of a secret code of sorts, and if he’d had any interest in continuing in academia he most likely would have chosen that as his research topic.

"Haikas,” Phainon heard Mydei mutter under his breath.

The two had gotten closer these past months; it had been over a month and a half since that night when they’d sparred for the first time, and they had fallen into a comfortable routine of bickering, sparring and working together with relative ease. If Mydei was uncomfortable with the amount of time they spent together, he didn’t show it—as much as Mydei acted like Phainon’s presence was an unbearable pain, he still ate with him and Castorice every day, and even waited for Phainon to finish eating so they could walk to evening briefings together.

Mydei’s morning training sessions even expanded to include Phainon; instead of training separately they now spent their mornings sparring after a quick breakfast. Phainon had made noticeable improvements; he noticed his balance getting steadier after every session, and was even able to predict Mydei’s movements to a degree after so long training alongside the other.

Now, midway through the Month of Weaving, Phainon felt at ease. The Month of Reaping had passed slowly, but eventually faded into the cooler, breezy days of Mnestia’s domain, taking with it the sharpest memories plaguing Phainon’s mind.

With Mydeimos by his side, soaking in the early autumn warmth, Phainon felt more himself than he had in a long time. The days passed by uneventfully, and as much as Phainon welcomed the quiet, he was itching for something exciting to sink his teeth into. Sparring with Mydei helped scratch that itch but only temporarily, making Phainon approach every spar with a vicious excitement.

As if the Titans had been listening to his thoughts and decided to grant his wish, Phainon finally spotted movement in the trees nearby. He readied his greatsword in an instant, Mydeimos moving at the exact same time, having heard the rustling of leaves and responding instinctively.

Giving chase, the two of them raced through the trees, whipping through bushes and orange-leaved branches alike. The Titankin was fast, but not fast enough; before long Phainon and Mydei had caught up to it and disposed of it with little more than a few slashes of their blades. They found several more Titankin nearby, tracking their trail until they found what looked like the biggest camp.

Clearing the camp took little time at all, and the two fought monster after monster until the clearing was completely silent, monster remains and thick splatters of black blood the only proof that the camp had once existed.

Phainon wiped the blood off of his sword as best he could, but knew he’d have to give it a thorough cleaning once they returned to Okhema. He looked over at Mydei, who was shaking the blood from his gauntlets, crimson markings gleaming in the sun.

Phainon couldn’t help but be curious. He didn’t quite know what the markings were—were they paint? Or were they possibly inked onto Mydei’s skin? He didn’t realize he was staring until Mydei cleared his throat, and Phainon’s awareness returned to him in a jolt.

”Ah—my apologies, Mydeimos,” Phainon managed. “I’m just a little curious… Are those tattoos? On your skin, I mean.”

Mydei looked down at the crimson whorls adorning his skin, seemingly lost in thought. He didn’t say anything at first, and Phainon was almost about to change the subject when Mydei finally spoke.

“These are a relic from my time in the Sea of Souls,” he said.

The little Phainon knew about Mydei from before coming to Okhema was taken from stories, legends of the immortal prince of Castrum Kremnos. Apparently, Mydei had been thrown into the Sea of Souls by his own father in a fit of madness, before the mad king slaughtered Queen Gorgo in a fight to the death.

“Ah,” Phainon said weakly. “It’s not really that important—”

Mydei cut him off with a shake of his head. “It’s all right.”

“My father tossed me into the Sea of Souls when I was eight,” he continued. “I did not emerge for nine years, and when I rose from the waters these markings had already appeared.” Mydei’s voice grew distant, recalling.

“There was a prophecy made when I was born. That I would grow up to murder my father and lead the Kremnoan dynasty into ruin. Perhaps it was fate that saved my body from crumbling into dust at the first touch of those frigid waters, but others say that it was my strength of will that allowed me to endure. That, I do not know,” Mydei answered the unspoken question honestly. “Whichever it was, I arose with a body that no longer bleeds or dies, and these markings are only a reminder of the fate which binds me to a kingdom that no longer exists.”

“Do they hurt?”

Mydei looked at him strangely, and Phainon rushed to clarify. “I mean, the markings being a reminder of your past, the prophecy…” If it were Phainon, he wouldn’t want to look in the mirror and see remnants of a fate he was trying to forget.

Mydei seemed to get what Phainon was trying to say. “Yes. But every day they hurt a little less.”

Phainon understood. He, too, knew the pain of being the last of his line, of having no place to call home. He knew what a lonely burden it was to bear.

Mydei said no more, and Phainon gazed at him. A man destined for murder and strife, cursed to outlive everyone he knew, forced to wander the rest of his life. And yet, not cowed by fear or burden, just…undeniably alive. It brought a sharp ache to Phainon’s chest, and he rubbed at it absentmindedly.

Something about Mydeimos intrigued Phainon, the more he learned about him. As talented as Mydei was at fighting, he was not bloodthirsty, or violent. In both duties and battle he was meticulous and thorough, and he always fought with every ounce of his strength, but it was never out of a desire to cause pain or to vent his anger. When Phainon gazed at Mydei, all he could see was nobility, and strength—the strength of Mydei’s will, perhaps, but also of his character.

Phainon wasn’t sure he’d ever met someone as captivating as Mydei. The way he looked, the way he fought, the way he moved through a world that seemed to hold only cruelty for him.

“You’re staring, Deliverer,” said Mydei.

“I was just thinking… You fight so beautifully,” Phainon said.

“That again. If you say it again I’ll think you actually mean it.”

“I do mean it,” said Phainon.

Mydei stared at him, his golden eyes glinting with something unknown. After a moment, he turned away. “Let’s go back.”

Phainon got up, heart thumping strangely in his chest. The autumn light seemed to have cast a strange glow upon Phainon’s thoughts, but he pushed it out of his mind as they returned to the city together.

After returning to Okhema that day, Mydei began avoiding Phainon.

Phainon first noticed something was wrong the next day at lunch. They had sparred as usual that morning, and while Phainon noticed Mydei was quieter than usual he didn’t think anything to be out of the ordinary. Mydei speaking somewhat freely was still a relatively new occurrence, after all.

But when Mydei chose to sit in the far corner of the canteen instead of beside Phainon, where he had sat for the past few months, the message was clear.

Castorice saw where Phainon was staring across the room and followed his gaze. “What did you do?”

Phainon’s gaze snapped back to her. “Nothing!” he said indignantly. “Why would this be my fault?”

“Whose else would it be?” replied Castorice, looking back over at Mydei, her brow furrowed in concern.

She was most likely right, but Phainon didn’t like it. Nor did he know what to do about it. Phainon replayed his actions of the last few days. Had one of his jokes gone a little too far?

Nothing particularly offensive came to mind. Phainon kept wracking his brain all through lunch, but by the time he looked back over at Mydei, the other had already left.

The rest of the day passed the same. The two of them were not assigned duties together the rest of the day, but Phainon noticed how Mydei did not meet his gaze as they would pass in the corridors.

Phainon didn’t know what to do, and he returned home that evening feeling frustrated and confused. Just the day before, he’d felt as if Mydei had finally become a friend, only to turn around and treat Phainon more distantly than he had in months.

That night, Phainon’s dreams were restless. He woke the next morning earlier than usual, feeling ill at ease.

Phainon still went to the training arena that morning, seeing that Mydei was, predictably, already there. However, Mydei surprised him by looking him straight in the eye when he arrived, acknowledging him with a nod.

“Let’s begin.”

Stunned, Phainon could say nothing, so he readied his sword.

They sparred as if nothing had changed, the familiar sound of clashing swords breaking the silence of the quiet morning. After the dust settled, however, and Mydei left in the direction of the palace alone, Phainon saw Mydei’s face had reverted back to his silent, emotionless visage. The face that had been so animated during their fight was now an empty husk, and Phainon did not know how he could return it to what it once was.

Thick clouds of hurt and confusion flooded Phainon, clogging his senses. He couldn’t focus on anything all day, almost knocking poor Trianne into the baths as he carelessly turned a corner with a heavy crate in his arms during morning duties, failing to see her in his path as he trudged down the corridor, blinded by his heavy thoughts.

This went on for a whole week. Mydei stopped eating meals in the canteen altogether, and withdrew from the rest of the Chrysos Heirs entirely. The past few months, Mydei had on occasion been seen secretly helping with the dromases, and feeding them extra treats, but even that seemed to be no more.

Curiously, though, his spars with Phainon continued.

The two no longer spoke while they sparred, their challenging taunts and bickering nowhere to be found. Instead, their spars were silent but for the clash of their blades and the sound of their heavy breaths carrying through the air.

It was excruciating, but Phainon had no idea how to fix it.

It was only after a week of this that he decided their stalemate could not continue. Phainon felt like a coward to have avoided making a decision for so long, but a part of him had hoped that Mydei would come back by himself after a while, having realized how much he enjoyed having Phainon around.

Clearly, Mydei was not going to return on his own. Phainon made up his mind that he would speak to Mydei face-to-face, as he should have from the beginning.

chapters.title: Chapter 7
chapters.html:
“Phainon. A word?”

Phainon now stood, as he had many times before, in Aglaea’s office in the Hero’s Bath. Aglaea stood before him, drumming her fingers on her desk.

“You seem to be struggling with Mydeimos,” Aglaea said.

Ah. Phainon should have known Aglaea would be informed of every last occurrence within the Chrysos Heirs, her golden threads keeping her up to date with any minute shift in dynamics.

“That is correct, Lady Aglaea.”

Since making up his mind to confront Mydei the other day, Phainon hadn’t had any luck in speaking with him whatsoever. Mydei was not going so far as to completely avoid Phainon, but whenever Phainon approached him Mydei would brush him off with a dismissive, “Not now, Deliverer” or “I’m a little busy”.

The only time Mydei ever looked him in the eye nowadays was when they sparred, but that was not helpful in the least. No matter how much Phainon wanted things with Mydei to return back to normal, something about their spars felt sacred, and no matter how antithetical it seemed, Phainon could not bring himself to disrupt that.

Aglaea hummed musingly. “Well, I had hoped the two of you would be able to work things out sooner rather than later, but I suppose this’ll have to do. There has been an increase in the smuggling of valuable artifacts of late; I suspect there’s a larger organization behind it all. I’d like you and Mydeimos to investigate—find their hideout, and report back to me. Do you think you can do this?”

Phainon considered. “Yes,” he answered truthfully. Both he and Mydei were diligent, and Mydei wasn’t the type to let their recent strife interfere with a mission. And maybe Phainon could use this time with Mydei to finally iron things out.

“All right,” Aglaea said approvingly. “Be prepared to depart at sunrise. I will inform Mydeimos.”

By the same time the next day, Phainon severely regretted taking on the mission. Not only was the atmosphere between him and Mydei excruciatingly awkward, the mission itself was turning out to be extremely ill-fated.

The two of them were supposed to track the smugglers to their hideout, mark the location and report back to Aglaea. Unfortunately, the band of smugglers they were currently trailing had apparently been hiding in a series of tunnels underneath the hills a half-day’s journey from the city.

Phainon hated tunnels. He felt claustrophobic, and it was hard to breathe. Not just that, but he was pretty sure they were losing the trail, as he noticed what seemed to be the same fork in the tunnel for the second time.

“I think we’ve lost them,” Mydei spoke aloud.

Phainon huffed out a breath in frustration. “Yeah. I’m pretty sure we’re lost now, too.”

Earlier, on the road, Mydei had refused to respond to Phainon if he tried to talk about anything unrelated to the mission, so Phainon had reluctantly turned away from all personal talk. It didn’t make the situation any less frustrating, but at least the mission wasn’t completely silent.

They hadn’t had any time to come up with a new plan before Phainon heard scuffling behind them. He turned swiftly only to see one of the smugglers they had been tracking behind them. The smuggler, clearly surprised to have found others in the tunnels, stopped in his tracks when he saw Phainon and Mydei before bolting back the way he’d come.

Phainon cursed internally. Great. Now all their work would be undone, and they’d have to report back to Aglaea that they’d blown the mission by getting lost and getting snuck up on by the very people they were supposed to be sneaking up on.

Phainon would have suggested they call it off and head back to the city, but remembered that they were still in the unfortunate position of not knowing where they were.

Out of nowhere, the ground began to shake, the tunnel walls trembling. Phainon fought to keep his balance, but then the ground collapsed beneath his feet, and he knew no more.

The first thing he was aware of was a heavy weight pressing on his entire body. The second was that he couldn’t breathe.

Phainon opened his eyes and could see nothing. Struggling, he attempted to shake off whatever was atop of him, but then immediately stopped, letting out a pained cry.

The weight wasn’t on his entire body after all, only his chest, his left arm and his left leg; as Phainon opened his eyes again and his vision adjusted to the darkness, he realized his chest and the left half of his body were covered in rubble.

Suddenly, he remembered. He and Mydei had fallen, so they must be underneath the tunnels.

Mydeimos. Phainon tried sitting up with a wince, and scanned the area they had fallen into for Mydei. He found him, lying next to Phainon’s feet, covered in just as much dirt and rubble as Phainon. Phainon couldn’t fully move, could only prop himself up on his elbow as he called out, voice creaky.

“Mydeimos.”

There was no answer.

Fuck. “Mydeimos!” he hissed.

Mydei groaned, finally rousing. Luckily, Mydei didn’t seem to be hurt, and the rubble hadn’t pinned any of his limbs to the ground, so he was able to sit up easily. He looked back for Phainon, apparently remembering the situation they were in, and their eyes met.

“Are you hurt?” Mydei called out tentatively, once he realized Phainon was conscious.

“N—yes,” Phainon almost denied it, but what good would it do? “I can’t move.”

Mydei got up, moving to Phainon’s side. “Are you?” Phainon asked, noticing how Mydei seemed a bit unsteady on his feet.

“Just bruised, I think,” Mydei said, and helped shift off the rubble from Phainon’s form. After a little bit Phainon could finally move, but sharp pain lanced through his left leg as he tried standing, causing him to hiss in pain.

“Here.” Mydei helped him stand, supporting Phainon so he could sit against a nearby wall. Phainon winced as he leaned against the wall, his left arm throbbing.

”You’re bleeding.” Phainon looked down at his arm, only now seeing the golden blood staining the white fabric of his coat, enough to make him feel a bit queasy.

”Oh,” Phainon said faintly. “That explains the pain.”

Mydei looked at him with what could only be a glare, but quickly retrieved the bandages from Phainon’s supplies, which luckily hadn’t been damaged in the fall. Phainon gritted his teeth as Mydei stripped off his bloodied coat from his arm and cleaned the wound. It was not shallow, and would take a while to fully heal—Phainon must have gotten the gash from the rocks that fell on top of him, but he hadn’t noticed the pain until just now.

After Phainon’s arm was bandaged, Mydei went to look for a way out of their current predicament, and Phainon took the opportunity to assess their surroundings.

They had fallen into a cave, which was about ten paces wide and five paces long, the ceiling maybe six paces above them. It seemed like the smuggler scout had triggered a cave-in; Phainon couldn’t see any source of light or a hole where they might have fallen from, and the pile of debris on the ground was substantial.

Mydei kept looking for an exit, but as time passed and Phainon’s heart grew heavier, he couldn’t help but feel helpless.

There was no way out. They were completely, thoroughly trapped.

Phainon balled his fist and hit the ground in frustration. Why didn’t anything seem to go right anymore? These recent weeks had just been one headache after another, starting with the person sitting to Phainon’s left.

Mydei had evidently given up searching for a way out; he was now sitting against the cave wall, eyes closed.

Phainon looked over at him, the frustration in his chest welling up, mixing with the anger that had been dormant these past few days. He tried so hard to keep it in, but ultimately failed.

“Why won’t you talk to me anymore?”

Mydei kept his eyes closed, but noticeably stiffened. He didn’t answer.

Phainon was truly angry now. “Why won’t you look at me? You can’t ignore me now. We’re stuck here until we find a way out.”

Mydei opened his eyes but didn’t meet Phainon’s gaze, his eyes instead resting on Phainon’s greatsword where it lay a short distance from their feet.

“You still won’t speak to me? What, you can’t be honest unless you have a sword in your hand?”

Phainon realized the truth of it as the words fell out of his mouth. Mydei, who had been shifting to presumably avoid this conversation, froze.

That was it, wasn’t it? Mydei had never turned Phainon away when they sparred. He still looked Phainon in the eye during those quiet mornings, face alive and full of determination, eyes blazing with anticipation of the fight.

Mydei had always been honest in the arena.

Phainon didn’t know what to say, the words he might have spoken caught in his throat. It was silent again while Phainon sat, dumbly.

“You…” Mydei’s voice broke the quiet. Phainon’s head snapped over to look at Mydei. He hadn’t honestly expected Mydei to respond to that accusation.

“You remind me of my friend,” Mydei finished his thought, head leaning back against the cave wall so he was looking upward.

Phainon didn’t say anything, only watched as Mydei spoke to him, really spoke to him, for the first time in a week.

“I used to have friends, once. After I returned from the Sea of Souls, I spent some time gathering troops, amassing an army to retake Kremnos. I still had people, then. My teacher, Krateros, and my friends…” Mydei’s voice tightened as he continued.

“They were my closest companions. I had known all of them since I was young, and they supported me unconditionally, no matter what path I took.

“Perdikkas, he died first. Then Leonnius, Ptolemy, and Peucesta. And finally…it was Hephaestion that fell. I killed my father, then left. I didn’t have a home anymore anyways. Krateros… I didn’t tell him I was leaving. It would’ve made me reconsider, so I just left.

“I walked the earth for ten years. I tried to escape my past—live somewhere quiet, make an honest living, but it never felt right. So I kept wandering. When I came to Okhema, I met you and everyone else, and I thought maybe I could get by. I thought I didn’t need anyone, was past needing anyone, and so I kept being alone.

“But then you kept showing up around me, and talking to me, and I found myself thinking that maybe it was okay to have someone stick around. I thought it was okay, but—” Mydei’s voice broke. He still stared resolutely at the ceiling of the cave, but his voice shook minutely.

“But the way you looked at me, back in the forest, I saw it clearly for the first time. It looked exactly like how they looked at me, how he looked—” Mydei’s voice cut off as he stopped abruptly, looking down at his knees. After a few moments, he took a shaky breath and continued.

“I just…can’t lose another friend.”

Phainon’s heart had been near bursting with anger in the beginning, which had now turned into a sharp, unbearable ache in his chest. Now, he understood.

“So…” Phainon began through the thickness in his throat. “You’re saying we’ve actually been friends for a while.”

Mydei turned his head, finally looking Phainon in the eye. He said nothing, but his eyes were rimmed in red.

Phainon sat up straight, moving his body to face Mydei directly, being careful not to jostle his injured leg. “Mydei, I’m not going anywhere,” he promised with the full weight of everything he was feeling.

”If you need me to swear it, I will. I swear. I am never going anywhere. You will never, ever have to walk through this world alone. I will become strong enough to never falter, so you’ll never have to worry about being alone again. I’ll be worthy enough to stand by your side,” Phainon insisted.

Mydei didn’t say anything for one long, heavy moment. And then finally he responded, in a softer and more honest tone than Phainon had ever heard him use, “You already are.”

Phainon couldn’t respond for almost as long. Only after he cleared the lump in his throat away and hastily wiped his hand across his eyes did he say, fiercely, “Then you can’t ever ignore me again.”

“I won’t.”

“Ever.”

“Never again.”

“Then we’re friends now, Mydei. You know that, right?”

“...Yeah, I know.”
