chapters.title: Chapter 8
chapters.html:
After that, they sat in silence for a while. Phainon’s face felt warm with the acknowledgment of what just occurred—Mydei didn’t hate him. Mydei did like being around him. They were friends now, for real.

Phainon was lost in those happy thoughts for an embarrassing amount of time until Mydei spoke again.

“Now what?”

That brought Phainon’s attention back into focus. They were still stuck in the cave, far beneath the tunnels they had been lost in earlier, with no visible way out.

“Now… We find the way out?”

Phainon tried getting back to his feet, but he’d forgotten how bad a shape his leg was in, the movement setting off an intense bloom of pain underneath his skin, bringing him back to a sitting position with a gasp.

He couldn’t walk. At least, not at the moment.

Phainon let out a nervous laugh. “Ah, haha… Um, maybe I’ll leave that to you, Mydei.”

Mydei looked over at him, the barest hint of concern visible in the furrow of his brow, the usual gold of his eyes dulled in the darkness.

“Rest,” he said, and returned to his search for an exit.

Phainon rested, but he wasn’t happy about it. He hated sitting on the sidelines, wanted to help Mydei look for a way out. He didn’t have much hope that they would find one, but he didn’t want to think about that right now. Which was why helping Mydei would have been better and more efficient, if not for Phainon’s stupid injured leg.

As he sat there, Phainon watched Mydei. Mydei searched every corner of the cave, checking the places he’d searched earlier with thorough diligence. Phainon could only watch, and it wasn’t long before his eyes grew heavy with fatigue.

Phainon wasn’t aware of falling asleep, or of dreaming, but he woke with a start when he felt a hand upon his uninjured shoulder. He blinked sleepily and raised his head.

Mydei was looking down at him. “I found a way out.”

The so-called way out was yet another tunnel. Mydei had discovered it by pushing on the cave walls, trying to see if there were any hidden doors or escape routes—this tunnel had been disguised behind a makeshift wall of loose rock. The smugglers, or whoever created these tunnels, must come down here regularly, perhaps to free any unlucky kinsmen who had been caught in one of their intentional cave-ins.

Phainon stared at the tunnel entrance from where he stood next to Mydei in front of it. He knew he couldn’t complain, since they would probably be stuck down there to die otherwise, but he still hated it.

”I hate tunnels,” he grumbled under his breath as Mydei helped him limp into the darkness.

The tunnel was darker than the ones they had been in above, and damp; Phainon could vaguely make out the sound of water dripping the farther they made it into the tunnel.

The going was slow; Phainon’s leg allowed them to only move at about a snail’s pace. Phainon kept glancing at Mydei to see if he was annoyed by their limited speed, but luckily Mydei didn’t seem to mind. He stopped whenever Phainon’s breath got too ragged, or his steps got too uneven, and they kept moving forward like this for a long time.

Phainon didn’t know how long it had been since falling into the cave, and he hated not knowing. He just hated uncertainty in general—he wished there was some source of light they could see that could help reorient his body to his mind. The tunnel was leading them slightly upwards, so there was a chance it was leading them back to ground level, but there was no way to be sure. His head was pounding, and his vision was going a little fuzzy, but he just wanted out of these titansforsaken tunnels.

As he looked over at Mydei to check on his condition, Phainon’s eyes caught on Mydei’s hair. The red tips were slowly fading—Mydei would surely need to re-dye them soon. How often did he do that? The rest of his hair was the color of spun gold, glinting in the faint light —

Glinting in the light. Light.

Phainon’s eyes snapped back ahead of them, and he could see a distant fork in the tunnel, the first they had encountered since entering. And on the left side of the fork, there was light.

His heart soared. They had made it.

The new tunnel indeed led outside; Phainon was half-worried it would lead to another cave, or perhaps if they were extremely unlucky, right to the smuggler’s base, but it did not. Phainon had never been more happy to breathe fresh air.

The sun was high in the bright blue sky; they had been in the tunnels for at least a day, maybe two. They left the tunnels behind without a second thought, moving as far away from the hills as they could with Phainon’s condition.

It was less than a quint later, when Phainon’s leg threatened to give out from strain, that he and Mydei finally stopped to rest. They had made it to one of the forests circuiting the hills, and with the remainder of their supplies Mydei made a small camp.

Phainon had been moving forward purely on adrenaline, but now that they finally stopped he practically collapsed onto the bedroll Mydei had set out. His entire body ached, and his leg throbbed. He looked down and saw the bandages on his arm had been soaked through again, and every move of his head made it feel like it was rattling with crushed glass. Phainon let out a small noise of pain and frustration as he tried to get comfortable on the bedroll, very quickly finding it to be an impossible task.

Mydei looked over from where he was setting up his own bedroll, then came over to rest a hand on Phainon’s forehead. Brow furrowed, Mydei removed it after a short moment.

“Fever,” he said, and began redressing Phainon’s wounds.

As Mydei rewrapped his bandages, Phainon felt a sudden absence of warmth, and he shivered. Mydei noticed and stared at him questioningly.

“Cold,” Phainon managed out.

Mydei finished and laid him back down on his bedroll so he could rest, and Phainon’s eyes shut almost immediately, pulling him under to the shores of sleep. Before his consciousness abandoned him, he heard the shuffling of leaves, and the last thing he felt before falling asleep was the weight of a warm chest enveloping his back.

Phainon’s dreams were hazy, nondescript things. He knew he dreamed, but each fragment drifted away before his consciousness could anchor them to his memory. Phainon slept like this for an unknown amount of time, and when he finally woke, it was dark.

Phainon’s head felt foggy, his tongue thick in his mouth, and he felt like he hadn’t slept at all. His eyelids were incredibly heavy, but he had awoken to a terrible thirst, and he needed to drink something. Phainon tried to sit up, but found himself trapped. Through his haze, it took Phainon a few moments to realize that it was because someone’s hand was across his chest, preventing Phainon from moving.

Phainon finally registered the weight of someone lying behind him, chest to back, and he turned on his side as best he could.

The hand wasn’t just somebody’s. It was Mydei’s.

Mydeimos was asleep behind him, arm across Phainon’s front as Mydei held him to his chest. He had evidently pulled his bedroll next to Phainon’s to sleep next to him. It was immensely warm, and Phainon would have found it comfortable if not for the sudden realization that he was entirely too hot and completely drenched in his own sweat.

Water.

Suddenly reminded of the throbbing pain behind his eyes and the dryness of his throat, Phainon squirmed to release himself from Mydei’s grip, fumbling in the darkness for his canteen. His fingers reached through the darkness, searching for the press of cool metal against his fingertips, but—

Mydei stirred behind him.

“Phainon?”

Phainon stilled. “I need water,” he whispered, his voice cracked through with dryness.

Mydei rose, the heat against Phainon’s back returning for a brief moment, and Phainon swallowed. His head pulsed with exertion, and he was too tired to do anything but watch as Mydei stood and retrieved his canteen from where it had been hiding. He held it to Phainon’s lips and allowed him to drink, water dribbling down Phainon’s chin after he gulped down several grateful swallows, only stopping when Mydei pulled the canteen away.

Mydei stoppered the canteen and put it down, and then his hand made its way onto Phainon’s forehead. It stayed there for a moment until Mydei finally retrieved it, his eyes somewhat displeased.

“Your fever… It’s too high,” Mydei muttered, almost to himself.

Phainon watched through droopy eyes as Mydei went to rummage through their supplies, returning with more bandages and another one of their canteens. Phainon blinked heavily as he fought to stay awake, opening his eyes to look up at Mydei when he felt the coolness of a compress on his forehead.

Mydei was wiping the sweat from his brow, sharp eyes unreadable in the darkness. He noticed Phainon watching him, but only said, “Sleep.”

Phainon closed his eyes, and slept.

The next time Phainon woke, he did not see the yellow-red canopy of trees he had fallen asleep under, instead he woke up to see a ceiling. He was in a bedroom—not his, and neither was he in Okhema; as Phainon turned his head he saw a window on the adjacent wall, outside an unfamiliar landscape of trees and rolling hills.

His body didn’t feel as heavy, and his head felt lighter. Phainon was surprised that sitting up wasn’t difficult, and he lifted the covers to see his left arm had been wrapped in clean bandages once again.

The room was quiet, and Phainon was considering what to do next when the door to the bedroom suddenly opened.

It was Mydeimos. He looked cleaner, the dirt and grime from the last few days nowhere to be seen.

“Your fever got worse,” Mydei said, gesturing to the bedroom. “I found a house nearby and asked for a spare room and some medicine.”

“Ah,” Phainon said, the weakness in his voice surprising him. He cleared his throat and tried again, but his voice still came out raspy.

Mydei walked over to the side of the bed and handed Phainon a glass of water that had been set upon it. Phainon accepted it gratefully and drank, the coolness of the water soothing his throat.

Once he had drunk his fill, and Mydei returned the glass to the bedside table, Phainon felt a slow rush of embarrassment, brought on by the memories of the past few days.

“Um,” Phainon began. “I’m sorry.”

Mydei shook his head once. “No, I… I should have caught your fever earlier.”

Phainon shook his head, echoing Mydei. “No—you got us out of there, and I ended up not being able to help at all…”

Mydei lowered his head, as if deciding whether or not to shake the acknowledgement off, but ultimately returned his gaze to Phainon’s. Changing the subject, he asked, “How are you feeling?”

“Better,” Phainon answered honestly. “Not like death, anyway.”

Mydei looked him over once, assessing, then nodded, seeming accepting Phainon’s self-evaluation. “All right,” he said. “You should get more rest, and then we can return tomorrow.”

Phainon agreed. He felt infinitely better than he had in the forest, but he knew he shouldn’t push his body right away, even though he was itching to return to Okhema and his normal routine.

Before Mydei could leave, Phainon found the courage to speak up.

“Mydei?”

Mydei turned to look at him, hand on the doorknob.

“Thank you.”

Mydei gazed at him for a moment, then nodded, closing the door behind him as he left.

Phainon was sentenced to bed rest for the rest of the day, with plans to leave the next morning. Mydei slept in a cot in the corner of their room, refusing Phainon’s insistence that he should take the cot instead, as he didn’t feel sick anymore, and they left the next day after breakfast, making sure to thank the family whose spare room they had commandeered profusely.

Their hosts also insisted on sending them with a horse, given Phainon’s state, but relented after Phainon insisted he could walk without aid. His body was in much better shape than it had been days before, the pain in his arm and leg only mild, and his fever long gone.

The return journey took twice as long, since Phainon couldn’t maintain his usual speed with his weakened body, but the atmosphere between the two of them felt completely different than when they had set out only half a week before—instead of pained silence, conversation between Mydei and Phainon returned to a semblance of what it once was, and the conversation now flowed easily, a reminder of their newly forged friendship.

Mydei even smiled occasionally at some of Phainon’s stories, which made the idea that had half-formed in the back of Phainon’s head that he had imagined their conversation in the tunnels fully evaporate. The image of Mydei’s little half-smile made Phainon’s chest swell up with something unnameable, and Phainon kept telling more and more absurd stories in the hopes of seeing it again.

So it happened that when they arrived back in Okhema, they were both in good spirits, and Phainon was looking forward to the heaping plate of cheese pies he would devour when they returned.

The pair needed to report to Aglaea before they could be released to their own devices, so they headed to Aglaea’s office. As they rode the lift up to the Hero’s Bath, Phainon snuck a glance over at Mydei.

So much had changed during this mission, and Phainon couldn’t help but feel excited for what was to come. With Mydei by his side, he felt a sense of camaraderie and comfort, one he hadn’t felt since he was a child, running through the fields with Cyrene.

Everything was looking up.

As the lift reached the uppermost level of the baths, Phainon was startled to see Aglaea was already waiting for them. Except—no, she was talking with someone, a man Phainon didn’t recognize.

Mydei froze, and Phainon looked over to ask what was wrong, but the words died in his throat as he saw the stricken expression on Mydei’s face.

Aglaea and the stranger had noticed the arrival of the lift, and turned to face them both. The stranger’s eyes widened as he took in the sight, staring at Mydei where he stood at Phainon’s side.

“Mydeimos?”

Mydei’s throat bobbed. When he spoke, it was hoarse, and Phainon was surprised at how strained it sounded.

“Krateros.”

Krateros.

Phainon knew why that name sounded familiar. He had just heard it for the first time, only a few days ago.

My teacher, Mydei had said.

The teacher Mydei hadn’t seen since before he left Castrum Kremnos, ten years ago.

Mydei was still staring at Krateros, frozen with shock and uncertainty. It was silent for several long, thudding moments.

Until Krateros stepped forward—one step, then two, and then all of a sudden he was kneeling at Mydei’s feet.

“You’re alive,” Krateros breathed in relief.

Mydei still had not moved, but those words must have broken his hesitation, and he moved a hand to Krateros’ shoulder.

“Do not kneel for me, old friend,” Mydei said quietly.

Krateros rose to his feet. Now that he was standing closer, Phainon could make out his features—he was older, features grizzled with age and heavily scarred, remnants of the Kremnoan legacy present on almost every visible patch of skin. He wore the same dark crimson that Mydei did, edged in gold with foreign designs woven through the fabric of his chiton.

Seeing Mydei and Krateros side by side, Phainon felt as though the legendary kingdom of Kremnos had come back to life, standing in front of him like a fairy tale made real.

Mydei did not seem like he knew what to say, and neither did Krateros. It had been ten years since their last meeting, after all, so Phainon supposed it was understandable that the words they might have said once could have gotten lost along the way.

Aglaea spoke. “Please, feel free to stay here as long as you need. I imagine you might have some catching up to do.” With that, she moved to depart, catching Phainon’s eye as she passed.

Phainon understood. This was not the time to stick his nose where it didn’t belong. He turned and went to the lift with Aglaea, watching Mydei’s back as the lift descended.

Aglaea and he were silent until they reached a quiet balcony of the palace where they could speak freely. When they arrived, Phainon recounted the events of their ill-fated mission, wincing as he told her about how he had been incapacitated with fever during most of it. Aglaea did not blame either of them for losing the smugglers’ trail within the tunnels, only acknowledged how shrewd the smugglers had been in choosing the location of their base.

After that, it was silent. Phainon didn’t know how to ask what he wanted to, so he said nothing. As always, though, Aglaea knew what thoughts brewed behind his thin facade, and spoke first.

“The Kremnoan detachment arrived yesterday, seeking refuge from the black tide after their settlement was destroyed.”

The black tide had been creeping closer and closer to Okhema in recent years—it was the very disaster that had destroyed Phainon’s home, yet still it spread chaos and destruction across the earth, no end to its vicious reign in sight.

Okhema had become a sort of refuge, taking in victims displaced by the black tide’s wrath, but the city walls were only so tall, the stones only so strong. One day, it would fall to the black tide. Phainon could only hope it wouldn’t be soon.

Phainon wondered. “Do they know? That Mydei—that Mydeimos is here?”

Aglaea shook her head. “No. Just Krateros. You saw him.”

“But they’ll know now.”

“I assume so, yes. Mydeimos… I cannot protect him anymore. This city knows him, and it is only a matter of time before his people learn he is here.”

“What will happen to him?” Mydei’s people must believe he abandoned them. Would they be angry? Would they demand answers?

“That, I do not know.”

Phainon wanted to know what Mydei was feeling at that moment. He excused himself and returned to his apartments, his appetite gone. All he could think about was Mydei.

Mydei had left his people after the fall of Kremnos to live his own life and escape the fate that shackled him to a ruined kingdom. Now that his people were here, in Okhema, what would happen? Would Mydei be once again forced under the burden of leading his people? But Kremnos no longer existed, had been gone for a decade.

Would Mydei be allowed to go free? To live for himself?

Phainon couldn’t free his thoughts from this perilous chain of thinking, and he ached restlessly for hours. No news came from Mydei or Aglaea, and Phainon found himself going to eat dinner on his own in the market, jittery with uncertainty.

He had just sat down at an unoccupied table beside the market stall to eat his bowl of stew when he heard a group of people rustling to sit down at the table behind him. They were being loud, and as much as Phainon tried to ignore them he was ultimately unsuccessful.

Perhaps that was for the better, for what they were talking about made him stop dead, the spoonful of stew that had been halfway to his mouth freezing in midair.

“What’s taking Krateros so long?” one of them grumbled.

“Who knows? It’s not like complaining about it will do any good.”

“Forgive me if I don’t want to spend more time in this damned city. It’s bad enough Krateros led us here.”

“Where else would we go, Nikias? If you haven’t noticed, there aren’t that many places untouched by the black tide nowadays,” another piped in, sounding annoyed.

“Perhaps, but Okhema?” Nikias hissed. “You know what they think of our people. We’d be better off almost anywhere else, black tide be damned.”

Phainon’s heart felt impossibly loud. These were Mydei’s people. He shoveled the stew down his throat. He couldn’t stand worrying about Mydei any longer, and finished his dinner as fast as he could stomach.

Without looking behind him, Phainon left the market, and went searching for Mydei.

He wasn’t in the baths. The Hero’s Bath was empty, as was Aglaea’s office—Phainon had peeked in guiltily, not wanting to snoop where he wasn’t allowed, but the room was empty. He checked the canteen, too, but Mydei wasn’t there.

Besides Mydei’s apartments, where Phainon had never been, that only left one place.

When Phainon arrived at the training arena, Mydei was sitting on one of the wooden benches surrounding the ring. The tension in Phainon’s heart released somewhat, a tightness he didn’t realize he was carrying. Outwardly, Mydei looked fine, but Phainon knew that didn’t mean the inside was necessarily the same.

Mydei looked up as Phainon came over to sit beside him.

“Are you okay?” Phainon asked.

Mydei gazed at him. “I don’t know,” he answered.

Phainon reached over to clasp his shoulder, squeezing it firmly. He said nothing for a moment, letting his hand rest on Mydei’s shoulder, and Mydei did not brush it away.

After a moment, Mydei spoke again.

“He doesn’t blame me for leaving.”

“Krateros?”

Mydei nodded. “He said…he understood. That I needed to leave.”

Phainon said nothing.

“I spent so long wondering what I would say if I ever saw him again, saw my people again. I ended up not being able to say a thing. He said he was hurt, in the beginning, that I didn’t tell him. He said he forgave me.”

Mydei’s gaze returned to where it had been, looking upwards toward the stars as he so often did.

“But my people did not.”

Phainon thought of Nikias, of the Kremnoans he had heard at the market. Were they still waiting for the day their prince would come to unite his kingdom, for the day Strife would return to the earth?

“Ten years is a long time,” Phainon said. “Do they still cling to their hopes of returning home?”

“I don’t,” Mydei responded. “But I never did. I left to forge my own path, after all.”

Phainon thought of his own yearning, the ache he felt whenever he remembered Aedes Elysiae, how much he wished to return to that idyllic time.

“I would. Cling, I mean. I still do.”

“To tell the truth… I think I do, too. I never truly wished for the crown, never wished to bear the burden of Strife—but Kremnos was my home,” Mydei said wistfully. “If there was someone in front of me who had the power to bring me home, I would cling on to them, too.”

Mydei’s hand reached up to grasp Phainon’s where it still sat on his shoulder.

“What should I do?” he asked quietly, almost whispering as he looked over at Phainon.

“What do you want to do?” asked Phainon, softly.

Mydei’s golden eyes rippled with remorse, guilt, and finally—resolve.

“I want to stay.”

“Then stay.”

Mydei squeezed his hand, then released it, his gaze returning to the night sky.

“I hope I can,” he said. “But…”

Phainon’s heart missed a beat.

“But?”

“I need to set my people free, first,” Mydei finished.

“How?” Phainon wondered.

Mydei let out a soft breath. “Krateros said I should do what I think is right. Letting my people continue to hold on to a fantasy is cruel. They need to be shown that it is time to move on.”

“He sounds wise,” Phainon said.

Mydei nodded. “He is. He taught me to read, to fight—everything I know, I learned from him.”

“Would he support you, then? In freeing your people?”

“I believe so, yes.”

“Then I agree. Do what you feel is right, Mydei,” declared Phainon.

The corners of Mydei’s mouth twitched up into a smile.

“I think I will.”

The next morning, Phainon was only somewhat surprised to see that Mydei was not at their usual spot in the training arena when he arrived. Phainon trained regardless, needing to feel his body move through the familiar motions of his routine. He had a hunch he would need some grounding before whatever Mydei decided to do happened.

Since Mydei wasn’t there, Phainon knew he must have made up his mind.

Phainon couldn’t help but feel the threads of anxiety slither into his mind, but it was outweighed by the trust he had in Mydei. Mydei would do what was best—and as for what that was, only Mydei knew. This both soothed and worried Phainon, but he tried his best to focus on his forms, stubbornly setting his mind elsewhere to avoid falling into his thoughts.

The dam broke after breakfast. Phainon was finishing up his meal in the marketplace when a courier came with a summons from Aglaea.

All Chrysos Heirs must be present, the courier had said.

Phainon’s pulse felt too quick. This was it.

He made his way to the Hero’s Bath, and found the rest of the Chrysos Heirs had all arrived before him, gathered in Aglaea’s office. Castorice, Hyacine, Cipher, the Tribioses, even Professor Anaxa—Phainon hadn’t known the professor was even in Okhema at the moment. Even so, his heart gladdened to see all of them together again.

Mydei stood beside Aglaea, the morning sun filtering through the large windows, casting radiant beams of light upon his golden hair.

Like a crown of gold, Phainon thought to himself.

Mydei greeted him with a slight nod, his head aglow at the movement. Then, Aglaea spoke.

"Thank you all for coming here so early in the day. I hope all of you have eaten, for this will not be a particularly short meeting. Today," she cast her gaze upon Mydei, standing by her side, "Mydeimos has something to say."

Mydei did not falter as all the eyes in the room swung onto him. He stood straight, posture upright and regal, no trace of hesitation in his gaze as he spoke.

"I have not been truthful about who I am."

And so he told them. Mydei spoke about who he truly was, how he came to leave Kremnos, and how he found himself in Okhema. Mydei spoke the longest he ever had to anyone besides Phainon, and even though Phainon knew everything already, had been the first to know, his heart still thudded painfully with the knowledge of Mydei’s burdens.

The son of Strife, now in service to his kingdom’s age-old enemy.

And yet, Mydei wanted to stay. Perhaps that was what gave Mydei the courage to make this proclamation, to resolutely face his past in front of everyone around him—Mydei was not a cowardly man, but Phainon knew just how long he had been wandering in avoidance of his birthright.

After Mydei finished, he said nothing more, but did not leave either. He did not lower his head as if awaiting judgement, only looked upon all of them, at all the people he avoided knowing, the people he would have rather kept from knowing himself.

Cipher was the first to speak. "So the little lion was a prince all along, hmm? I should have seen that coming."

After that, it was like all of the tension hissed out of the room, and all of them spoke at once.

"De… You’ve been here so long and didn’t feel like you could tell us, huh. I wish… I wish you knew how much we care about you!" said Tribbie, a little teary.

Trinnon piped up, "Yeah! It’s okay you couldn’t tell us… We don’t care about that. We just want to support you, and even though you’re a prince that won’t change!"

The corners of Mydei’s eyes crinkled as he looked down at the three Tribioses, his eyes softening with warmth. Phainon was amazed to see that Mydei was actually smiling. Phainon had seen the sight only a few times before, and was shocked that Mydei was smiling here, in front of the Chrysos Heirs.

Something in Phainon disliked seeing Mydei smile so freely, in front of people he scarcely knew, as if his smile should belong to quiet moments alone—not a resource to be handed out so easily. And yet Mydei’s smile brightened him, made him shine so intensely, so much so that Phainon couldn’t keep following that train of thought. Still, a strange feeling nested within Phainon as he watched Mydei.

Amidst the hubbub, Castorice made her way to Phainon’s side. Phainon greeted her with a quick smile, but his gaze quickly returned to Mydei.

Seeing he was not going to speak first, Castorice spoke up.

"You knew already, didn’t you?"

Phainon tore his eyes from Mydei and looked at her, a small smile returning to his face, this time one of guilt.

"...Perhaps."

Castorice let out a small sigh, folding her arms in front of her. "You two always were close. I should have known you’d be keeping secrets from the rest of us."

"They were Mydei’s secrets, not mine,” Phainon protested halfheartedly, but not with any real emphasis behind his words. He felt as though a great weight had been lifted from his heart, seeing all of his friends and fellow companions receive Mydei with such care. He hadn’t really thought Mydei would ever be rejected by any of them, but it still brought warmth to his chest to see it unfold.

"I know," Castorice said, turning to face Phainon, looking him in the eye. "I’m just…really happy to see you the way you are now. Both of you," she glanced in Mydei’s direction. "I didn’t like to see you so unhappy… Before you left, I mean."

Phainon knew she meant before he and Mydei had left on their cursed mission to the smuggler’s caves. A lot had changed in such a short time, and Phainon felt so full, with the knowledge that he had someone such as Mydei around him.

"I’m glad to see him this way, too," Phainon answered honestly. Surrounded by the Chrysos Heirs, the Tribioses pulling on his gauntlets, Aglaea’s eyes glimmering with mirth, Professor Anaxa standing haughtily out of the way of the commotion—Mydei was still there, smiling, being seen for the man he truly was. Not his past, but not just a reflection of all Mydei wanted to be, either—all of it.

Mydei looked...at peace.

At that moment, Mydei looked up, his gaze connecting with Phainon’s, and the golden light of the morning sun reflected off of Mydei’s hair once again, blinding Phainon, causing him to wince and blink away in avoidance. When he looked back up again, Mydei was still looking at him, the corners of his lips pulled up in a smirk as he snorted.

Phainon felt affronted. Mydei was laughing? At him? He turned to Castorice instead, forcing away the childish impulse to pout. His heart felt too fast, as if he’d been running.

Phainon could only stand by the side with Castorice for the remainder of the meeting.

The announcement was planned for later the same day, at the height of Ascent Hour. That did not give the Heirs much time to plan, but all of them sprung into action to begin preparations. Even Anaxa stepped up, refusing to stand by even though he had little relationship with Mydei other than in the color of their blood—Anaxa had not been to Okhema since before Mydei’s arrival, so the two had never crossed paths.

And yet, Anaxa surprisingly did not bristle when Aglaea requested he deliver the invitation to the detachment. Normally, the cantankerous professor would turn up his nose at tasks that he deemed beneath him, usually when they had no relation to his research, but this time he only agreed amicably.

Phainon was astounded. He had never seen the professor seem so… Was 'passive' the correct term in this case?

He found a moment, in between his own rushed duties that morning, to ask the professor before he set out to meet Krateros.

"Professor… I’m curious. Why…"

"Why am I assisting in this endeavor? I am not so obstinate a man, Phainon."

There was nothing Phainon could say that was polite to that, so he kept his mouth shut.

"I only wish to wrap things up here smoothly so that I may return to the Grove. I do have a responsibility to this city, and I don’t know where you get the idea that I want Okhema to fall to ruin while I’m not around. If this doesn’t go well, and Okhema burns to ashes due to the heat of Kremnoan flames, where else would I get my research funding?"

Phainon should have known. He sighed, and went back to his duties.

When the time finally slipped by into Ascent Hour, the chimes tolling in the distance, Phainon steeled his heart, readying his mind.

It was time for Mydei to meet the detachment.

Only Phainon and Aglaea were to accompany him, as the nature of Mydei’s proclamation had little to do with the Chrysos Heirs as a whole. Phainon would only be there as Aglaea’s unofficial successor; if Aglaea hadn’t been preparing him to lead the Heirs once she lost what remained of her humanity, even Phainon would not be present.

Phainon hurried to the room they had arranged to meet in. Mydei had said that in the time preceding the fall of Castrum Kremnos, the Kremnoan detachment was at its height, with hundreds of troops marching under Mydei’s banner. After Kremnos fell, the detachment did not disperse, but many left to live their own lives, wandering as Mydei had across the earth in search of a new beginning.

Still, though, there were those who remained. The detachment today was dozens strong, still led by Krateros, who had been unwilling to abandon the remains of his people. During Mydei’s talk with Krateros, the latter had told him that the detachment had found a town willing to take them in, where they settled down. It was three years after Kremnos’ fall, and they set up camp, aiding the village and slowly creating a home of their own.

It had been peaceful, Krateros said. But nothing lasted forever—for what village could hope to defend against an enemy as shapeless and vindictive as the black tide?

Seven years after rebuilding their home from scratch, the Kremnoans were once again forced to watch as their home burned to the ground.

That is how the detachment now found its way to Okhema, and back to its crown prince. If Phainon were Kremnoan, he would feel it was some machination of fate, that Mydei would truly be the one to deliver their salvation and bring them back home, restoring Kremnos to its rightful glory.

Phainon’s chest twinged. He shook it off as he finally arrived at his destination, standing outside the grand doors emblazoned with a golden sun for a moment to catch his breath.

Then, steeling his resolve, he pushed in.

Aglaea had not yet arrived, and neither had Mydei. The feasting hall was filled with dozens of soldiers garbed in various shades of red and brown. Many of them looked in high spirits, jeering and laughing over each other.

But still there were those that were quiet; as he walked towards the front of the hall, Phainon noticed a group noticeably out of place near the front of the room, faces grim as they murmured amongst themselves.

He had little time to acclimate himself to the boisterous atmosphere, however, as just then Aglaea entered from a door across the hall with Krateros, walking over to where Phainon stood. Krateros acknowledged him with a courteous nod, and Aglaea passed her gaze over him noncommittally.

The hall quieted as the soldiers noticed the appearance of their superior, but was not entirely devoid of noise, mumbled whispers and laughter still audible across the large room.

Then, the door from which Aglaea had entered swung open once again, and Mydei stepped into full view of the detachment.

The hall went silent. Mydei approached the front of the hall and addressed them all.

"I am Mydeimos, Crown Prince of Castrum Kremnos. Today, you shall witness me accept my birthright as king of Kremnos."

The hall erupted with noise, expressions of shock and disbelief present on the Kremnoans. Phainon noticed how the group in the front of the room did not join the commotion, but their faces darkened with anger as they recognized their prince.

Mydei spoke again, his voice carrying over the noise, although he had not spoken any louder than before.

"My first decree as king will also be my last. The Kremnoan dynasty ends here."

The hall was suddenly silent again, the soldiers shocked into a mute daze. Then—

"You abandon your people, your birthright, just like this? How can you call yourself a true Kremnoan as you run away from your duty?" came an angry voice from the soldiers. It was one of the soldiers who had looked angry at Mydei’s arrival, who had not joined the others in loudly voicing their surprise.

And… Phainon recognized that voice. It was one of the voices he had heard in the market the day before—Nikias. The one who had sounded disgusted by being forced to crawl to Okhema for aid, the home of their greatest enemy.

Mydei looked at Nikias impassively, no trace of anger or guilt in his expression.

"I have never wished to carry on the glory of Strife. It destroyed my father, and it destroyed the legacy of Kremnos. There is no honor to be found in bloodshed, only pain. I only wish for all of you to live for yourselves as you have never done, as your kinsmen have done—as I have done."

Nikias glowered, still standing in opposition to Mydei.

"That is not who we are. Kremnoans were born to follow Strife, would rather die than run from their birthright, tails between their legs," he hissed. Nikias’ face was red, but he still spoke clearly and loud enough for the entire hall to hear, every word dripping with contempt.

"The prince who abandoned us once is abandoning us once again. Legends speak of the sting of betrayal, but there was never a betrayal as legendary as this," Nikias spat. "I would never abandon our people, nor become as cowardly as you, Mydeimos."

With that, Nikias spun on his heel and marched out of the feasting hall, half a dozen others following him out.

Then, it was silent once more.

After a few moments, it did not seem like there would be any more outbursts. Mydei simply stood silently, not offering any more explanation than he already had. The hall felt humid, tension thick in the air.

Krateros moved first. Without saying anything, he turned from beside Mydeimos to face him, and then fell to one knee, head bowed. For a beat, nothing happened, and then—

As if they had only been waiting for permission, the Kremnoan detachment followed suit, kneeling to Mydei.

It was not all at once, but rather staggered; Phainon could see the less fervent soldiers at the back hesitate for a moment, but by the end there was not a single Kremnoan soldier who was not kneeling.

The Kremnoans bowed to no one but their leader—their king.

Mydei’s people had forgiven him, after all.

Phainon’s chest swelled with emotion. Besides Nikias and his group of radicals, it seemed Mydei did not need to fear his people’s derision. They might still be angry, upset at Mydei for finding his own place, but still they knelt.

Mydei looked over his people, and if Phainon knew him any less, he might have missed the glint of triumph in Mydei’s eyes.

After, food was brought out, and they all ate together. Aglaea had made sure to prepare the ariston in advance, planning for the possibility that all would go well. Phainon hadn’t entirely known what to expect, but he was glad the meeting with the detachment hadn’t ended in bloodshed.

Phainon sat at Mydei’s table, with Krateros and Aglaea, and they were joined by an endless stream of soldiers as they cycled by, wanting to catch the attentions of Mydeimos himself. No matter that Kremnos no longer stood, and Mydeimos had been a king for less than a quint— the soldiers looked at Mydeimos like he was made of the sun itself, as if stars would fall from the sky if he only willed it.

Through it all, Mydei talked, clapped shoulders, even huffed out a short laugh or two. From where he sat across the table, Phainon could hear when he slipped into the foreign sounds of what must be Kremnoan with his comrades, speaking lowly and intimately with some, raucously and boisterous with others.

It was a long time before the food had been cleared away and the line of Mydei’s admirers receded, leaving Phainon thoroughly exhausted. He excused himself when he saw there was nothing left for him to do, planning on returning to his apartments to sleep before evening duties. Mydei was still speaking with Krateros as Phainon left, the doors swinging shut behind him.

Phainon was almost home, taking the quickest route through the city’s back alleys when he heard it—a muffled shout, and a thud, accompanied by jeers. Phainon followed the noise and rounded a corner into a narrow alley, running into a group of men.

One of them was on the ground, covered in dirt and blood, and the others stood over him, garbed in familiar robes of crimson.

“Oh, look, it’s Mydeimos’ little bitch,” Nikias said, his voice dripping with condescension. He was leaning against the alley wall, looking at Phainon with a nasty glint in his eye.

“Violence is prohibited inside city walls,” Phainon said, eyes narrowing. “Disperse.”

One of the other men scoffed. “What are you gonna do, Deliverer? We are not Okheman citizens—you cannot punish us, no matter how much you wish to.”

Phainon’s voice came out harder than he meant it to. “Okheman or not, you are still subject to Okheman laws.”

Nikias pushed off the wall, stepping closer to Phainon. “Again, what are you gonna do?” he sneered. “If I say this man attacked us first, you wouldn’t believe me, would you? You’d say that I started it, that because I’m Kremnoan that I must have thrown the first punch.”

“You don’t know that,” Phainon said. “Regardless of who punched first, you shouldn’t have returned it.”

Phainon moved to pick up the man from the ground, and was startled to see that it was Hesiodos, the man who oversaw the dromas workshop. The older man’s face was darkened with dirt and blood, his left eye blackened.

“Hesiodos,” he murmured, astonished. “Are you all right?”

The old man lifted his head weakly. “Yes,” he breathed.

Phainon’s chest throbbed. Hesiodos had always been kind to Phainon—he’d always greet Phainon with a smile when he passed by, or offer him fruits from his garden as payment for helping around the workshop.

“Are you well enough to return on your own?”

“Yes,” Hesiodos nodded. He started to hobble off in the direction of the market before he stopped, turning once more.

“Thank you, Lord Phainon.”

Phainon watched him leave before turning back to the Kremnoans. Nikias and his gang hadn’t left; they either hadn’t been smart enough to scurry away while Phainon was distracted or were stupid enough to choose not to. Whatever the case was, they were still there, and Phainon was not in the mood to be polite for much longer.

Facing the Kremnoans, Phainon crossed his arms across his chest. “I cannot protect you from the consequences of your actions—I will have to question both you and Hesiodos to find out what happened. Regardless, you may be punished for raising your hand against a member of this city.”

At the word “protect”, Nikias’ face screwed up into a scowl. “You wish to protect us, Okheman? What makes you think we need your flimsy protection?”

With that, Nikias stepped into Phainon’s space, and Phainon’s heart thudded dully in his chest. He didn’t think Nikias truly wanted to harm him, but he had not brought his greatsword to the meeting with the detachment in the name of diplomacy—which meant he was very much unarmed. If Nikias wanted to harm him, Phainon would have to rely on his hands to stop him.

Nikias stepped forward until Phainon’s back was against the alley wall. Phainon willed his face to remain impassive, but he had stupidly walked into this situation without an ace up his sleeve, and he felt the danger of it now.

“You are Mydeimos’ people,” Phainon said, looking Nikias in the eye. The other Kremnoans stood back, watching them, ready to fight if Phainon so much as breathed wrong. “I do not wish you to come to harm.”

“Mydeimos’ people… We are not his any longer,” Nikias spat. “That traitor abandoned us once again. He has no claim over us any longer, nor on the throne of Kremnos.”

Nikias shifted, and Phainon stilled as he felt the cold metal of a blade against his neck.

“How would dear Mydeimos feel if he found all of his new friends dead? Hmm?” Nikias dug the tip of the blade into Phainon’s skin, and Phainon felt dizzy as he felt it break skin, the pain like lightning across his neck.

Fuck. He had to get out of here, now.

Phainon naively hadn’t expected the situation to deteriorate this quickly, and his senses must have still been dulled by his fever the previous week to have failed to alert him to the current danger before it got to this level.

He couldn’t die here, unarmed in an alley, far from anyone who would hear him cry out in pain.

He couldn’t do that to Mydei.

Phainon’s mind raced, trying to think of a way out of his current predicament, when he heard footsteps coming from the alley entrance. Nikias and the others clearly heard it too, and Nikias quickly lowered the blade from Phainon’s neck, keeping it out of sight in between their stomachs.

Before Phainon could think about using this to his advantage, the person belonging to the footsteps came into vision, and Phainon was distracted by the sight of Mydei in front of him, his eyes on Phainon, eyes narrowing as he registered the nature of the situation.

Seeing Mydei distracted Phainon for a moment, and he shifted on his feet, forgetting for a moment the danger he was in. Phainon heard a quick gasp, and then realized the sound came from his own throat.

Phainon’s breath caught as he felt a sharp, excruciating burst of pain, and he looked down, confused—until he saw Nikias’ dagger where it rested hilt-deep in his abdomen.

He couldn’t process it, couldn’t really understand what was going on, but one moment Phainon was upright, the next he was on the ground, coughing out dirt where he had inhaled it. Nikias stood over him, face struck with horror, as if he hadn’t actually meant to stab— stab?—Phainon.

Phainon had been stabbed.

Oh, fuck. Being stabbed fucking hurt.

Nikias was gone, the others were gone, all Phainon saw was Mydei. Mydei’s face was in front of him, eyes wide, frantic. He was saying something but Phainon couldn’t hear it, the blood in his head was rushing too loud, drowning out everything else.

Phainon’s vision was going spotty. Fuck. This couldn’t be it.

Phainon felt pressure on his hand, looked down to see Mydei’s hand encircling it, squeezing it. The other was on Phainon’s stomach, staunching the flow of golden blood. Mydei was frantic, his eyes searching Phainon’s, his mouth still moving, words unceasing.

Slowly, Phainon’s hearing returned, and he heard what Mydei was saying.

“You’re stronger than this, Deliverer. You do not get to die here. Stay awake, just—stay awake.”

Mydei’s voice was thick, as if he was speaking through a lump in his throat. Hearing that, Phainon tried to shake off his daze and struggled to speak.

“I…”

Mydei looked at him, eyes unsure, fearful.

Phainon tried again.

“Not…going anywhere… Promise.”

Mydei’s eyes softened, and he squeezed Phainon’s hand again, stronger. He said something else, but Phainon couldn’t hear anything more, and all he saw was blackness.

For a while, all Phainon knew was pain.

The first time he woke up, all he could feel was red-hot fire across his abdomen, spreading from his chest to his navel. It burned, and Phainon thrashed to try to put the fire out, but that only made it worse, and he cried in search of relief until it came in the form of sleep, putting him out of his misery.

The second time, something cool was wiping across his face. Phainon wanted to see what it was but couldn’t figure out how to open his eyes, and the darkness pulled him under again before he could remember.

The third time, someone was opening his mouth and pouring something in.

“Please swallow, Lord Phainon,” they whispered. Phainon swallowed, and then slept.

The fourth time, Phainon woke up on his own. His eyes opened without issue, and he blinked, his eyes taking a moment to adjust to the light. He was in the Okheman infirmary, the blue- and white-striped beds a familiar sight from when he used to get in fights after training as a boy and had to come to the infirmary for pain-relief patches, or poultices for his wounds.

“Lord Phainon!” came a gasp from beside him. Phainon turned his head to see Hyacine, standing next to his bed where she stood fiddling with some vials, which she promptly put down in favor of holding his hands tightly.

“How are you feeling?” she asked, face knitted with concern, her green eyes blinking furiously.

Phainon went to speak and found his voice hoarse with disuse. “All right… I think.”

That was true. He wasn’t in much pain, besides the muted throbbing of his abdomen, and he didn’t feel uncomfortable anywhere else.

“I’m so glad you’re okay, Lord Phainon,” Hyacine squeezed his hands, mouth turned down in a frown. “I…did my best, but you almost didn’t… If you’d been stabbed just a little higher, I might not have been able to heal you,” she said, sounding like she was about to cry.

Phainon felt a rush of affection. Hyacine tried her best to heal every patient with a smile, and for her to be brought down so by Phainon’s condition—Phainon felt sorry for having brought her to this state.

“But you did, Miss Hyacine. I’m sorry,” he admitted. “I should have been more careful.”

“You should have,” came a voice from the door.

Mydei was standing at the door, arms full with what looked like gift baskets full of fruit and get-well charms.

Phainon couldn’t say anything for a moment, his breath caught in his throat as he remembered his last moments with Mydei.

Mydei had looked so, so sad.

But Phainon hadn’t broken his promise. He was still here.

Phainon sat up straighter in his bed as Mydei approached, setting the gift baskets on the nightstand closest to Phainon’s bed.

Phainon attempted to break the silence, and couldn’t help but tease.

“Decided to bring me some gifts, my dear Mydeimos?”

As much as he tried to make it sound lighthearted, the teasing fell flat, and came out clumsier than Phainon had planned.

Mydei didn’t glare at him, but it was a near thing.

“Tribbie, Trianne, and Trinnon asked me to bring these over for you. Said you needed to take care of your health while you recovered.”

“I’ll leave you to it, then. I’ll be back to check in on you later, Lord Phainon,” said Hyacine with a small smile, releasing his hands as she left, saying hello to Mydei as she passed by.

Mydei greeted her with a nod, and Hyacine was gone.

Not saying anything, Mydei sat down in the chair next to Phainon’s bed. Phainon felt the inexplicable urge to fill the silence, as he often did when things felt awkward.

“I—um, I’m…”

Mydei broke through his stuttering. “How…are you feeling?”

“Good. I mean, okay. It doesn’t really hurt now,” said Phainon, tripping over his words. He wanted to be honest with Mydei—too often, he told white lies in front of others to not make them worry. Things like, I’m doing well, or I’m okay, don’t worry.

He didn’t want to lie to Mydei.

Mydei affirmed this with a nod. “Hyacine said she gave you some medicine to ease the pain.”

Phainon had figured; his body felt lazy in ways that could not be attributed to sleep, his muscles too slow to react. He was grateful for the relief from pain, and his torso throbbed almost in spite, as if Phainon’s body could guess what his attention was focused on.

It was quiet between the two of them, and Phainon didn’t know what to say.

Aren’t you glad I’m not dead? I didn’t break my promise and leave you behind, Mydei. Didn’t I do well?

What in Kephale’s name would Mydei say to that?

A bolt of inspiration struck Phainon. “Nikias…” he began.

“He turned himself in.”

“What?”

“He said he hadn’t meant to hurt you, and that he only wanted to scare you,” Mydei said, eyes sharp in anger.

Phainon recalled the look on Nikias’ face after he stabbed him, the horror and fear clear in Nikias’ eyes. He believed Nikias’ words—that was not the face of a man who wished to kill.

“Then… The others?”

“Followed Nikias. They are in Aglaea’s custody as we speak.”

“Did you…” Phainon couldn’t stop himself from being nosy. “Know them? Before?”

Mydei sighed, moving his gaze upward to stare at the ceiling. “Did I? I might have. Nikias, I never met. The others… Menander, Aristeides—their names feel familiar. But Euphranor… I think I knew him.” Mydei’s voice was sorrowful as he sorted through long-forgotten memories.

“If my memories do not fail me, he was the son of one of my father’s councilors. We played together, as children.” Mydei frowned. “His father earnestly supported the king and his violent policies, but back then, Euphranor was only a child. He would not have known of such things. To think… He would stand before me now and oppose me, just as his father would have, were he around.”

Phainon was suddenly reminded of the complexities of Mydei’s upbringing, ones he could not hope to relate to. He frowned at the thought of Mydei having to confront old companions, standing at opposite banks of a rushing river, forced to be at odds due to no fault of his own.

Lost in thought, Phainon was suddenly brought back to awareness by the feeling of Mydei’s finger poking the furrow of his brow.

“Do not worry for me, Deliverer, when you are in no position to do so,” said Mydei.

Phainon cast his head down, ashamed. Mydei’s statement gave him the courage to bring up what he hadn’t the courage to earlier.

“I’m sorry.”

Mydei did not ask what he was apologizing for, which made Phainon feel somewhat worse. But Mydei did not let him wallow, only replied, “You need not apologize for staying alive.”

“I was careless. If you had not been there, I—” Phainon’s throat threatened to close up, so he stopped mid-sentence.

“Hesiodos came and fetched me,” came Mydei’s reply.

Phainon stared at him. “What?”

“I was searching for you, and someone had seen you pass by that area, so I was close by. Then, Hesiodos came up to me and asked me to help you.”

Phainon had never felt so grateful for Hesiodos. If not for Mydei searching for him at that very moment, Phainon might not be having this conversation with him in the present.

He breathed out a sigh of relief, dropping his head in his hands.

“I’m just… Glad I didn’t have to break my promise.”

“You didn’t.”

Phainon looked up to see Mydei gazing at him softly, eyes devoid of the anger they had held previously. All of a sudden, his heartbeat felt too fast, his face too warm, and the memories of Mydei holding him to sleep while Phainon was in the throes of fever came to mind, unbidden.

Phainon flushed, and he turned his face away to hide, hoping Mydei couldn’t hear the stuttering pace of his heartbeat.

Luckily, Mydei hadn’t noticed—at least, he said nothing to betray his observations, so Phainon pushed those thoughts away as best he could, choosing instead to fiddle with the blankets.

Mydei surprised him yet again, however, as he reached over to grasp one of Phainon’s hands, holding it tightly. Phainon was startled into looking back up at him, and saw only immense care in Mydei’s eyes.

“Thank you,” said Mydei. “For keeping your promise.”

Phainon nodded, his mind too jumbled up to speak.

For now, that would be enough.

Chapter Notes

hoo boy has it really been almost a month... the daily grind has me within its clutches and i am powerless before it. please forgive me

Phainon was sentenced to bed rest for three weeks. Naturally, that meant he was walking around Okhema by the middle of the second, having whined and pouted his way into the nurses’ sympathies, who finally gave in and let him out of bed when they couldn’t stand his lonely, mournful expressions any longer.

Although he was upright, he was still forbidden from strenuous activity until Hyacine approved, meaning not even the city guards were willing to risk the healer’s stern retaliation by allowing Phainon into the barracks or the training arena.

Even Mydei did not give in, casting Phainon an even glare when he suggested a light spar after lunch one day. Phainon knew Mydei well enough to know that he was fighting a losing battle, and begrudgingly gave up, choosing to walk away instead.

In this way, the months slowly passed, the painted leaves of autumn giving way to the smell of damp and decay, finally settling into the brisk chill of early winter. Phainon’s wound had mostly ceased its throbbing, only making its presence known when he pushed himself too much, or lifted something too high above his head. He considered himself mostly fully healed, but the mostly part of that statement hurt his pride more than he wanted to admit, and so he didn’t mention that fact to anyone else.

The Kremnoans had not left. Not even after Nikias’ assault on Phainon, which nearly drove the Kremnoans out of the city in shame—Aglaea had welcomed the Kremnoans into Okhema with open arms, offering protection and belonging to whomever wished to stay.

Phainon saw them about the city increasingly often now, relaxing in the public baths or taking meals in the market. Slowly but surely, the Kremnoans were making themselves comfortable in the foreign city.

Not to say that it was a painless process—the Chrysos Heirs had needed to resolve many more disputes as the Kremnoans learned how to coexist with the Okheman citizens, and so Phainon had practically mediated more legal disputes in the last several weeks than in his entire career.

As for Nikias, he was originally supposed to have been exiled for assault of a Chrysos Heir, but instead he had spent only a few nights in the city jail. To everyone’s surprise, it was Phainon who had requested the lighter sentence—Phainon did not believe Nikias intended to injure him, and that stabbing Phainon was a mistake borne out of fear and anger. A dangerous mistake, but a mistake nonetheless.

Still, Phainon hadn’t seen Nikias since.

Now, the month of Fortune was halfway gone, and Phainon was looking forward to the festival held every year on the last week of the frosty month, when the city streets would fill with street vendors and the smell of treats roasted with honey, or the heady scent of spiced wine and seasoned lamb. Last year, Phainon and Castorice had roamed the busy streets in search of the best spiced wine, and were only distracted from their quest when they were drunk enough to have forgotten the reason for their excursion, giggling and stumbling through the city without a care in the world.

This month was under the rule of Zagreus, and so at first glance the month of Fortune would appear to be a misnomer, but instead it was the month of gamblers and chance. Whether your fortune was good or bad, this month would make it known, and the Festival of Fortune was full of fortune-tellers and games of luck, with everyone eager to see how their futures would unfold.

Phainon loved it. It always made for a festive atmosphere, and it was one of his favorite times of the year. He and Castorice had invited Mydei along this time, and Mydei, quite surprisingly, did not turn up his nose at the invitation, only huffing out a noise of affirmation.

When the first day of the festival arrived, Phainon left for the marketplace after dinner, where the heart of the festivities were set up. The streets were blanketed with snow, the light of the lanterns strung up throughout the streets and alleys reflected cheerily upon it, making it seem as if the entire city was bathed in gentle, golden light.

Merchants always went all out for the Festival of Fortune, working as hard as they could to pull in customers during the festival. Everywhere Phainon looked, he saw colorful lanterns and paper ribbons strung up above the dozens of stalls. Already, the festival was bustling with people, the atmosphere a pleasant hum.

Phainon’s breath frosted in the air as he breathed out, tugging his woolen himation tighter to his body. He had planned to meet Castorice and Mydei at the entrance to the market, but the two of them were nowhere to be seen.

Right as Phainon decided to find himself a better vantage point to look for them, he felt a presence behind him, and turned to see the very people he had been looking for.

“Finally!” grumbled Phainon. “I almost froze to death waiting for you two.”

“Oh, sorry. I ran into Mydei on the way, and we got distracted,” said Castorice, not sounding sorry in the least for Phainon’s plight.

“Hmmph.” Phainon turned to Mydei, who despite the chill was barely dressed warmer than his usual attire, only donning a thin woolen cloak over his light chiton.

Did Kremnoans not get cold? Perhaps the true heat of Kremnos was hidden within the blood of their king.

Phainon’s teeth chattered. He felt slightly envious of not needing piles of layers to keep warm, but shoved the thought away.

“Let’s get going.”

The atmosphere of the festival was as cheery as ever, and Phainon felt refreshed almost immediately. The past weeks had gotten increasingly busy, what with managing the Kremnoans and preparing for the month of Fortune, which always brought its own challenges as people settled debts, made new investments, or renegotiated contracts.

The three of them bought treats to snack on as they wandered through the market, Phainon and Castorice opting to grab mugs of spiced wine as well, while Mydei chose to drink warmed pomegranate juice instead, requesting the seller to add some fresh goat cheese.

When Phainon made a face at that, Mydei offered Phainon a sip, to which Phainon hurriedly refused. Maybe next time, Phainon said, knowing there would most definitely be no day where he tried that particular combination.

In the middle of the packed streets were various street performers. When they happened upon a bard strumming their lyre, singing a doleful tune, they stopped to listen for a while. It was a retelling of an ancient myth, tragic and heartwrenching. When the last note of the song rang out through the air, the crowd of people who had gathered to listen burst into enthusiastic applause.

After that, the bard launched into a joyful melody, the story a comedic tale of a mouse’s birthday celebration gone wrong, complete with uninvited guests, forgotten presents and decorations that kept disappearing.

The song made Phainon chuckle, and he turned to Mydei, mind suddenly consumed with a question he had never thought to ask.

“That reminds me, Mydeimos… When is your birthday? I don’t recall you ever mentioning it.”

Mydei replied after a moment, “It…passed. Last month.”

Phainon startled. “Last month?”

“It was the day after the first snow.”

“…Ah.”

Phainon didn’t know why he was upset by this.

“How did you celebrate it?”

Mydei tipped his head up, remembering.

“We ate dinner together. Me and Krateros.”

“Oh. That’s…good.”

That’s good you didn’t spend it alone, Phainon wanted to say.

For that was what had been bothering him. If Mydei hadn’t spent his birthday with Phainon, who else would he spend it with? He was not known to linger amongst others. But Phainon had forgotten—Mydei wasn’t alone anymore, not with Krateros and his people in the city.

Mydei must have sensed there was more hidden behind Phainon’s silence.

“Do not waste your time worrying about me, Deliverer. I am not one of those prattling fools who insist on being paraded around and pandered to on their birthday.”

Phainon still felt unsatisfied. He went to protest again but was interrupted.

“If this matter troubles you so, then I will save some time for you next year. That way, I can spend my birthday however you deem appropriate.”

Mydei’s words were sarcastic, but Phainon answered as if he did not pick up the underlying meaning behind his words.

“All right.”

To his credit, Mydei did not look surprised, only huffed out a quiet laugh through his nose.

“…All right, then.”

Belatedly, Phainon realized the space on his other side was suspiciously empty—Castorice was not beside him as she had been when they’d originally stopped to listen to the bard.

It took nearly half a quint to find her, as she had been corralled into a fortune-telling booth in a quiet alley not far from where they were watching the performance. She had apparently been enticed into entering with promises of a free divination, the merchant seemingly hell-bent on luring in a fresh customer. Unluckily for him, Castorice’s curse meant that she would not allow him to read her palm.

Castorice had been afflicted with a strange curse since birth; she could not touch others with her hands, unless she wanted to send them to an early death. However, the heavier the touch, the worse the effects—if she brushed against someone by accident, it wouldn’t kill them, only make them drowsy, but if her hands made direct, prolonged contact with someone’s skin, it would send them into a quick, albeit painless, death.

Phainon had learned very quickly to avoid touching Castorice casually, as the first few times he did it without thinking caused him to doze off right at the breakfast table.

In the end, the merchant ended up shooing them away, proclaiming bad luck in store for each of them, sore for the lack of profit to be made.

With that, they continued walking through the market, their contented breaths fogging out in front of them, visible manifestations of their presences on this cold, joyful evening.

When the air grew colder, and the lights of the festival began to blink out as stalls closed for the night, they decided it was time to go home.

They walked back together, and Castorice was the first to depart when they arrived at Marmoreal Palace. That left only Phainon and Mydei, alone in the darkness.

The city was quiet at night, the only noises being the occasional group of people returning to their homes from the festival, muted laughter and the crunch of boots on the snow.

Phainon said his goodbyes to Mydei, but found the other following him after he began walking away, and turned to face Mydei curiously.

Mydei stopped in his tracks, face impassive.

“I live this way as well.”

So they walked together, comfortably silent. Phainon’s heart and belly were content with the atmosphere of the festival, and he did not feel the need to fill the silence. They walked for a while, Phainon’s head lost in his thoughts until he realized they had passed Phainon’s apartments and were now in a corner of the city he wasn’t familiar with.

Phainon stopped in his tracks. They had arrived in an enclosed courtyard, the red door of a house barely visible through the branches of the snow-laden trees.

“Is this your house?” Phainon asked. He had never seen where Mydei lived before, and was curious.

Mydei nodded.

“Then… I should get back,” Phainon said, suddenly embarrassed. He hadn’t meant to keep walking with Mydei, lost in his thoughts, and the night was chilly. He shivered.

“All right.”

Mydei turned to go inside, and Phainon was struck with the urge to say something more before he left.

“Thank you for coming today.”

Mydei turned back, the hint of a smile visible through the crinkle of his eyes.

“I had fun. Thank you for inviting me.”

Possessed by a sudden need to make his feelings known, Phainon burst out, “You’re my closest friend, you know.”

Mydei didn’t say anything immediately. And then, “I feel the same, Deliverer.”

That was the answer Phainon had wanted, but somehow he was still restless. He didn’t know how to express what he was feeling, so he just stood there, struck dumb.

It was silent for a few moments until Mydei spoke again, still staring at Phainon.

“If…there ever comes a day where I lose control, when Strife overtakes me, I want you to kill me.”

Phainon stared.

“What,” he whispered, his voice cracking.

Mydei stepped closer to Phainon and took his hand, guiding it to a spot slightly above the small of Mydei’s back. Phainon could feel the heat of Mydei’s skin through his cloak, the distant pulsing of his heartbeat.

“My tenth thoracic vertebrae. If you pierce my body here, I will die,” Mydei said. “A true death—one my immortal body cannot evade.”

Phainon couldn’t move. He imagined his greatsword slicing through Mydei’s flesh, a shower of golden blood spraying through the air, and then Mydei, limp and unmoving, never to rise again.

Phainon stepped away quickly, removing his hand from Mydei’s back.

“No,” he said. “I cannot.”

“I would trust no one else with this,” said Mydei.

Phainon did not want to think about Mydei dying. He knew Mydei had died before, but Phainon had never witnessed it—besides, Mydei had said this would be a “true death”.

Phainon had lost enough.

“No,” he said again, turning away from Mydei.

“Deliverer,” Mydei stepped back into his line of sight, leading Phainon’s gaze back to his own.

“Only you are my equal in this life. Only you can get close enough to kill me.”

“I do not wish to kill you, Mydeimos!” Phainon roared. “There is no one I would rather kill less, and I would rather throw myself in front of another blade before I ran my sword through your back like a coward.” These last words burst out of him with vicious force.

“Phainon,” Mydei said firmly.

Phainon was trembling. He was angry, angry that Mydei did not see the weight of asking this of Phainon. He couldn’t speak anymore, choked by a lump in his throat, so he stood silently, glaring at Mydei.

Mydei was still looking at Phainon with the same indifferent gaze he always wore. It should have made Phainon madder, but the longer Phainon glared at Mydei the more he felt his anger slip away like a piece of driftwood in a fast-moving stream.

Only you are my equal.

Mydei feared losing himself to Strife, feared losing the iron grip on his control as much as Phainon feared losing his own. Phainon pictured it suddenly—if Mydei were to lose sight of himself after bearing the coreflame, there would be no telling how great the devastation would be. Mydei was the strongest warrior Phainon knew, and although he had never lost control before, if the coreflame was too much, then who knows how far he would go in the throes of madness?

Phainon’s throat was dry, so he swallowed.

“All right,” he said hoarsely.

Mydei still held his gaze, unwavering.

“I’ll do it.”
