The next few days kept Phainon busy, busy enough that he shouldn’t have had time to worry about other things, but his promise to Mydei kept returning to his mind whenever he had a moment to himself.

It was infuriating, but no matter how many times Phainon replayed the conversation, he still did not feel any more at ease.

Phainon wouldn’t go back on his promise, no—once he promised something, there was no chance of him failing to accomplish it.

It was just that Phainon didn’t want to think of Mydei dying.

Phainon had seen a lot of death, had killed hundreds of monsters for his pledge to protect the Holy City, but never before had he killed an innocent—never before had he killed a friend.

He knew he needed to take these feelings and plunge them deeper into his chest, so deep they wouldn’t come back to haunt him until later, as he did with most things that troubled him, but these particular feelings did not go easily.

For the time being, Phainon was stuck with this aching, claustrophobic feeling that came to mind whenever he remembered his promise to Mydei, which was often. So Phainon did as he did best—threw himself into his duties, volunteered for as many extra tasks as he could without collapsing, and forcibly filled his mind with nothing but work.

Fortunately for Phainon, it seemed to be working.

He didn’t think about it while feeding the chimeras that morning. He didn’t think about it while helping around the dromas workshop. He didn’t think about it during the weekly briefing on the black tide, or while out on evening patrol, or while making himself dinner that night.

Luckily for Phainon—who hadn’t been thinking about his promise to Mydei at all—he was soon presented with a pressing issue to solve.

The Kremnoans were planning to revolt.

Not all of them—several months had passed since the detachment’s arrival in the Holy City, and the cracks in the system were beginning to show. The Okhemans were beginning to lose their patience in accommodating the newcomers; likewise, the Kremnoans were becoming frustrated with the cultural barriers as they acclimated to their new lives.

The last few days, there had been whispers in Okhema of overthrowing the false king of Kremnos, who had led the Kremnoans to a doomed existence in the city of their enemy.

“I don’t understand,” Phainon said in their next meeting. “If they don’t like it here, why don’t they just leave? Why revolt?”

Aglaea frowned. “It seems simple when you put it like that, but I’m afraid there must be more to it. Mydeimos?” she asked, deferring to the Kremmoan sitting to her left.

Mydei considered for a moment before speaking, his golden eyes narrowing. “When I accepted the throne of Kremnos, there were many who opposed me. Even though most of my people accepted my order for them to live in accordance with their own wishes, perhaps my authority is not as absolute as I once thought. If my people doubt their king’s authority, then will they still follow his will?”

“Even if his will was for them to make their own choices?” Phainon asked.

“It seems as though no matter whether they accepted Mydei as their king then, they are struggling to accept his will now, now that they are encountering more issues in their daily lives,” Castorice replied.

“Then it would seem they need a reminder,” Phainon said. “Of who their king truly is, and whether he can be trusted to lead them to a better life.”

“It would seem so,” agreed Aglaea. “Does anyone have any suggestions?”

Silence. And then—

“A duel.”

All eyes turned to Mydeimos.

“A duel between the king of Kremnos and Okhema’s strongest warrior,” said Mydei, as he turned to face Phainon, determination burning in his eyes.

Phainon’s heart jumped. He would never refuse Mydei a duel, regardless of how high the stakes, but the thing he decidedly hadn’t been thinking about the last several days still squeezed at his heart, causing him to pause.

“Phainon?”

“Yes,” he blurted out.

Mydei nodded approvingly, his eyes never leaving Phainon. “Regardless of whether I win or lose, I know I can trust you to give me a worthy fight. I will prove to my people that my word is still true through the glory of battle.”

Later, Phainon asked Mydei something that had been on his mind the whole meeting.

“I thought you’d stepped away from the crown after your decree, Mydeimos.”

Mydei leveled a gaze at him. “I had. But if that decree never truly reached the hearts of my people, I still see it as my duty to enforce it. I will show my people the way to freedom, whether they wish to follow it or not. But if they have lost their way, it is my responsibility to show them the path once again.”

This made Phainon stop in his tracks for a moment, considering.

“But… Does this not mean that you will never stop being their king?”

“...That may be. But if that is what it takes to show them a new way, then so be it.”

Mydei had wanted to set his people free so he could live a new life, but for that he had to willingly shackle himself to the fates of the Kremnoan people to lead them into a new era.

It was a contradiction for the ages. Phainon’s head hurt.

After that, preparations for the duel began. It was scheduled for several days later, at the beginning of Entry Hour, so that word had enough time to spread through the nooks and crannies of Okhema, in hopes of attracting everyone they could to the match.

The day of the duel dawned bright and cold, the midwinter air biting as Phainon waited for the duel to begin. It was to be held in the dueling arena beside the barracks, which in recent years had been a popular venue for fighting tournaments and melees, as there was plenty of room for raucous crowds to gather in attendance.

Already, the stands were filled with Okhemans and Kremnoans alike, shades of blue and crimson mixing indiscriminately throughout the arena. Though the air was brisk, the sunlight was warm, and Phainon’s excitement vastly outweighed any nerves that might have been brought on by the crowd.

Finally, the judges arrived—Aglaea, Krateros, and a representative of the Council of Elders, acting as a neutral party. Mydei had arrived not long after Phainon, so with the arrival of the judges, the duel could begin.

Aglaea strode to the center of the arena and addressed the crowd, which quieted at the first resonant tones of her voice.

“Citizens of Okhema and guests of our esteemed city, welcome. Today, we bear witness to a battle of glory and strength between these two Chrysos Heirs. This duel shall showcase the strength of body and mind of Castrum Kremnos and of our Holy City. The victor shall receive a crown of laurels to commemorate their victory. However, regardless of the winner, I hope that this duel will prove that these two sides can indeed find common ground, and find mutual strength in each other.”

Raising her hand, Aglaea said, voice echoing throughout the arena, “Let the duel commence!”

With a blast of a horn, the duel began.

Normally, Phainon was the first to strike when they dueled, but this was the first time Phainon had been allowed to duel since being stabbed, and he was perhaps slightly out of balance.

It was immediately apparent that he had some catching up to do, as this time Mydei struck first.

Phainon was alert enough to not be caught by surprise, but his nerves tingled, alight with the change in pace. Mydei’s eyes glinted in anticipation as Phainon parried his strike, catching the shift in Phainon’s balance before he counterstruck, allowing Mydei to dodge unscathed.

Before Mydei had time to recover, Phainon took up the offensive, slashing at Mydei’s torso, but Mydei leaped back again, this time legs lashing out to sweep Phainon’s feet out from under him.

Phainon rolled with the momentum of the fall, rising on his knees to quickly block Mydei’s strike with the flat of his blade in the nick of time.

To anyone, they would look equally matched. Phainon knew it, and his blood buzzed with the thrill of the fight. He wanted to find out who would end up winning this time, far more than anyone watching in the stands.

Mydei’s eyes were brilliant, illuminated by the sunlight, and his immortal body gleamed with exertion, muscles rippling and twisting to avoid Phainon’s slashes, feet nimble and sturdy as they carried him through the steps of a dance only he knew.

He was beautiful like this, and Phainon felt once again as if he was locked in step with a being of legends, of divinity.

Phainon lost track of time, eagerly meeting Mydei’s blows with his own, until a horn blew and Phainon realized the day was over.

Curtain-Fall Hour had arrived, and the duel would be paused until daylight returned.

In bed that night, Phainon marveled. A whole day had passed, and yet he did not feel exhausted, only a little fatigued. He had never been one to slack on his training, but perhaps his stamina was heartier than he’d realized.

Phainon had expected to feel disappointed that he hadn’t been able to beat Mydei, though they had dueled all day. Instead, his entire body sparked with excitement.

Mydei was his equal in every way, matching him evenly strike for strike. They had fought for an entire day, and neither had won—and now, they got to do it all again tomorrow.

Phainon slept, spirit heartened by the thought. He would beat Mydeimos tomorrow.

Except he didn’t.

By the end of the second day, both of them were drenched in sweat and blood, but still standing.

By the end of the fourth day, Phainon wondered if the duel would ever end.

By the end of the seventh, Phainon was exhausted, but he was still determined to win. He would be the one to overthrow Mydeimos and his authority—show Okhema and Kremnos both who was truly the strongest warrior between them.

By the end of the ninth day, Phainon thought he might die if they fought for much longer. Every slash of his blade felt like it took all of his strength, and he was struggling to keep his balance. Still, Phainon persisted, and made it through the ninth day as he had the others.

The tenth day dawned chilly and gray, the arena shrouded in a dense fog that would have made Phainon shiver if he was still in touch with his corporeal form. He could only feel the urge to keep fighting, to win—and if he was sure of anything, Phainon would make sure this duel ended today.

With a blast of the horn, the duel resumed.

Phainon both wanted the duel to finish and for it to never end, so that he might have a chance to be locked in this battle of unmatched skill and raw strength for the rest of his life. As much as his muscles ached in protest, his lungs screaming for air, Phainon would have kept fighting day after day if only to just keep seeing Mydei like this.

For this was Mydei in his true essence—a being forged of strength and fire, his every move as swift and deadly as the lion of his birthright.

Phainon had never seen this Mydeimos. Mydei had always been fierce when they sparred, yes, and he would never have insulted Phainon by holding back, but this Mydei was something different entirely—something ancient and powerful, unable to be restrained by man or Titans alike.

Something…divine.

At that moment, Phainon realized Mydei’s tattoos were glowing.

The crimson tattoos swirling upon Mydei’s body were smoldering, now a brilliant red, the same tint as a glowing hearth. Not only that, but Mydei’s eyes, normally reminiscent of polished amber, were now the shade of burnished gold.

Upon noticing Phainon’s faltering steps, Mydei looked down at his body, seeing the changes for the first time. Smirking in realization, Mydei called out a taunt.

“So even Nikador believes we should hurry this up.”

Then, he flung his sword to the dirt, causing it to skid away, too far for him to retrieve without Phainon taking advantage of his weaponless condition.

“I can beat you faster with my hands, anyway.”

Snarling, Mydei pounced. He was quicker like this, refreshed as though they hadn’t been fighting for nine days straight.

Phainon struggled to evade Mydei’s blows, and was taken completely by surprise when Mydei flung out his hand and sent a flurry of crimson crystals flying toward Phainon.

He had no time to react, no time to process this new turn of events, and could only keep parrying. At first, Phainon had no hope of returning to the offensive, but soon he was able to avoid the crystals with ease, could sense Mydei’s next move and rush to meet him there.

At first, Phainon didn’t notice the red glow surrounding his body, nor the unnatural gleaming of his sword which had previously been dulled by the days of combat, but when he finally looked down and saw his arms ringed in a crimson aura, he didn’t have time to think about what it meant, only lunged at Mydei once more.

Phainon heard a maniacal chuckle, and somewhere in the back of his mind he realized it must have come from his own throat.

Gradually, the last of Phainon’s consciousness left him, and all he knew was the clang of steel meeting Mydei’s gauntlets and the thrill that grew intertwined with his heartbeat, pulsing happily with every shift of their feet upon the dirt.

In this way, the tenth day passed, and the horn blew, signaling the end of the duel for the day.

“Enough!” the representative from the Council of Elders cried out. “We will all die of hunger before this duel is decided. I wish to call for a draw.”

As the judges deliberated, Phainon stared at Mydei. The glow had mostly faded, but it was still there, outlining Mydei’s muscled figure with crimson. Mydei was staring right back, and Phainon knew his own glow must still be there, too.

”The judges have agreed. The result of this duel is a draw.”

There was the slight muttering of displeasure from the few spectators who must have remained, but Phainon wasn’t paying attention, his mind still hazy and red-tinted from the duel.

He couldn’t tear his eyes away from Mydei, who was shining under the moonlight with both a sheen of sweat and the remnants of his divine aura, whose eyes still remained on Phainon’s.

He couldn’t tear his mind away from the memory of their duel, the memory of Mydei meeting him at every strike, every movement of Mydei’s intertwining with his own.

They stood like that until everyone else had gone, with only the distant stars and the night wind to witness their presences.

Phainon didn’t remember leaving the dueling grounds, or how he made it home, only vague impressions of him and Mydei stumbling up the stairs to Phainon’s apartments, removing their clothes haphazardly and pulling their boots off without a care as to where they landed.

Phainon remembered pulling off Mydei’s gauntlets, holding him steady as Mydei lost his balance, delirious and battle-drunk, cheeks red with exertion. He remembered pulling Mydei into his arms as they toppled onto the bed, remembered running his fingers through the golden strands of Mydei’s hair as Mydei’s mouth found his neck, languid and sloppy.

He remembered pushing Mydei into the bed, inhaling his scent as he bit into Mydei’s skin, watching the crescents of broken skin close up in moments, and remembered biting more, until Mydei was shivering and moaning brokenly above him, fist tight in Phainon’s hair.

Phainon remembered being on his back, Mydei sitting above him, braid undone and face flushed.

Equal, he remembered Mydei murmuring into Phainon’s skin. My equal.

After that, Phainon remembered no more.

Phainon fucked up.

Phainon had severely fucked up.

He had awoken to the sun shining through the linen curtains, casting a warm luster onto the room. Phainon had felt sated, lazy in his comfort—until he noticed the presence beside him.

Mydei lay on the other side of Phainon’s bed, golden hair wispy on the pillows, his normally impassive expression muted in sleep.

Phainon’s heart thudded, and the spell was broken.

What had he done?

He couldn’t remember anything at first, didn’t recall anything past seeing Mydei’s form shrouded in crimson—until the memories came back to him in a rush.

Them leaving the dueling grounds together. Mydei, hands tangled in Phainon’s hair. Phainon, carving his teeth into Mydei’s skin.

Phainon’s heart threatened to stop, and he tried his best to be noiseless as he got up from the bed and went to wash his face.

When he returned to the bedroom, Mydei was sitting up, staring at Phainon.

Phainon didn’t know how he could salvage this.

“I—” he began, and then stopped.

Phainon couldn’t manage to say anything else, lost.

Mydei rose wordlessly. He began gathering his fallen clothing from the floor, and pulled on his boots without looking at Phainon.

Then, Mydei was gone.

“As for the blessing of Strife—”

Aglaea had called for a meeting not long after Entry Hour that day, intending on discussing the nature of the red glow that had surrounded both Mydei and Phainon during the duel. The Chrysos Heirs had collectively concluded that it must have been the result of a Titan’s blessing—Phainon had heard of loyal followers receiving divine favor in the form of a bountiful harvest, or coming into sudden and vast fortunes, but he had never seen it happen before his own eyes.

The Lance of Fury had apparently seen Mydeimos’ raw determination to best Phainon and sent him a blessing, granting him divine strength. Not only that, but Phainon had received Strife’s blessing as well.

Phainon registered this dully, but could not bring himself to focus on the conversation winding around him. He could only recall Mydei’s face as he left Phainon’s apartments that morning, the way he would not show Phainon his face as he walked out.

So even Nikador believes we should hurry this up.

Mydei had known the nature of the blessing from the beginning, and Phainon wondered if that meant he was resistant to the intoxicating effects Phainon had been on the receiving end of the day before.

Phainon recalled how it felt—dizzying, and freeing, as if every inhibition Phainon had ever constructed in his mind were felled in an instant. Were he in his right mind, Phainon would never have acted like that with Mydei.

He had never considered seeing Mydei that way, but now that he had, he couldn’t keep the thought of it out of his head.

Phainon dug his nails into his thigh, hard. Now was not the time, or the place.

But thoughts of Mydei lingered in Phainon’s mind through the rest of the meeting. Images of Mydei’s sleeping face, his mussed hair, but most insistent of all were Mydei’s eyes. Those golden eyes followed Phainon everywhere he went that day, no matter how much Phainon tried to shove them out of his mind as he went about his daily duties.

If the duel had achieved anything, it was that the appearance of Nikador’s favor had quelled all doubts of Mydei’s authority. No longer did the unhappiest Kremnoans look askance at the Okhemans, nor at the Chrysos Heirs—apparently assured of Mydei’s authority and therefore of Okhema’s trustworthiness, the few Kremnoans who had been threatening to overthrow their king had quieted down into reluctant submission.

Settling them down fully into Okhema would take a lot more time and effort, but for now, the Kremnoans were no longer an issue.

Phainon had gone the entire day pushing away thoughts of Mydei, so when Phainon saw a flash of golden hair turn a corner before him while walking through Marmoreal Palace after dinner, it took a moment for him to realize that it was the real thing.

Pulse racing, Phainon hurried after him.

“Mydei.”

Mydei did not turn around.

“Mydei,” Phainon said insistently.

At that, Mydei stopped, finally turning to face Phainon.

“...What.”

“Why did you leave?”

Mydei did not have to ask what he meant. They hadn’t spoken since that morning, and Phainon had felt like he hadn’t taken a deep breath all day for the tension.

“You didn’t want me there.”

“I… What?”

Mydei’s arms were crossed in front of him, the familiar position today seeming more like a barrier.

“Your face. You looked like you were about to apologize.”

Phainon had been. Mydei must have seen the confirmation in his face, for he made to turn around again and end the conversation. Seeing that, Phainon reached for Mydei’s arm, at the same time remembering the feel of Mydei’s skin under his touch, of the softness of his hair—

Mydei was staring at Phainon, an indescribable emotion flitting across his face as his eyes landed on Phainon’s grip on his arm.

“I—I’m sorry.” He was still going to say it, no matter whether Mydei wanted to hear it or not. “I shouldn’t have—shouldn’t have taken advantage of you like that—”

“Fool,” Mydei hissed, wrenching his arm out of Phainon’s grasp. “What do you think it means to be called an equal in Kremnos? Do you think me so weak as to let something happen to me that I did not wish to?”

With those confusing words, Mydei whirled back around and stalked away. Phainon watched him go, not knowing how to begin to process Mydei’s words.

Did that mean…?

Mydei had called him equal.

Phainon’s head spun. He needed to confirm something.

He found the professor in the library. Head buried in a book, Anaxa did not even bother to look up at Phainon as he pointed him in the direction of books on Kremnoan culture. Phainon didn’t take it personally—the professor had been conducting lots of experiments of late, seemingly due to an upcoming research presentation, so this state of intense focus was not an unfamiliar sight.

Phainon found the section on Castrum Kremnos with some difficulty; it was wedged between the folktale and geography sections, with only a sliver of the shelf belonging to Kremnoan customs. With a sigh, Phainon pulled out the small stack of books and plopped them onto a nearby desk, intending to pore through each of them until he found what he was looking for.

Phainon had not fully expected to find the answer in these books, but after only a little while of searching, he found it, hidden in a footnote in a book on the history of Castrum Kremnos.

Underneath a section on Kremnos’ worship of Strife, the footnote read:

“As such, the Kremnoan worship of battle has become closely intertwined with matters of love; in Kremnos, a comrade or sparring partner can only dream to be called another’s “equal”, the highest form of praise in Kremnos, as equality on the battlefield is seen to be the foremost marker of harmony between two individuals.”

Phainon closed the book, head spinning.

My equal, Mydei had said, under the influence of Nikador’s blessing.

You are my only equal in this life, Mydei had said before their fateful duel.

Mydei had called him an equal, multiple times.

Phainon left the library in a hurry, mind full of thoughts of equals and harmony.

Before long, Phainon found himself standing outside Mydei’s house, the painted red door the same as he remembered it, the trees bordering the courtyard still covered in snow.

He waited on Mydei’s doorstep for a long time, until the shadows had completely overtaken the courtyard, and the air grew chilly. Eventually, he rested his head on his legs, which he’d pulled closer to his chest to stave off the cold. He must have closed his eyes at one point, and only woke to the noise of someone’s footsteps on the snow before him.

He raised his head, strands of white hair falling to conceal his view.

He went to remove them from his vision, but the newcomer got there first, his leather gloves tucking the errant hairs behind Phainon’s ear.

Mydei stood before Phainon, breath frosting out in front of him.

Phainon was invited inside, Mydei giving only a cursory glance at Phainon’s condition before he demanded Phainon come in before he caught a cold.

Mydei’s home was not terribly large, and cozier than Phainon would have expected, with rugs blanketing the stone floor and patterned curtains drawn across the windows. The fire was low, with a pot of soup bubbling over it, diffusing the scent of lemongrass and basil through the house.

Phainon held his tongue until after Mydei had given him a blanket and a mug of honey mead and sat him down squarely on a tufted couch.

“You called me your equal.”

Mydei paused in his tidying of his living room for a moment, then resumed before sitting down beside Phainon.

“...Yes.”

Phainon didn’t back down.

“Did you mean it?”

Mydei looked him in the eyes, expression guarded.

“What are you truly asking?”

“Did you mean it?” Phainon pressed.

“Yes,” Mydei did not hesitate this time.

Phainon let out a shuddering breath, before he took his courage in hand once more.

“Did you mean it when you said you’d never let me do anything you didn’t want?”

Mydei’s eyes narrowed. “I didn’t mean that I’d let you, specifically—”

“Did you mean it?”

Silence. Then finally Mydei said, “Yes.”

Mydei was looking down into his own mug of honey mead when Phainon’s hands enclosed his, both of their hands wrapped around the mug.

Mydei looked up. Phainon had moved closer, so that their breaths were practically intermingled, their lips mere millimeters apart.

“Does that mean you’ll let me do this?” Phainon whispered.

In answer, Mydei exhaled softly, his breath warm on Phainon’s lips.

Then Mydei kissed him.

His lips were soft and warm and tasted like honey and pomegranate. Phainon couldn’t stop his hands from moving to cup Mydei’s face, brushing his thumbs over his cheeks as he kissed Mydei deeper.

The mug of honey brew was moved to the table, forgotten, as Mydei pulled Phainon closer to him so that their bodies were entwined and Mydei’s hands tangled in Phainon’s hair.

When finally they needed to come up for air, Mydei’s face was flushed, the reddest Phainon had ever seen it. He rested his forehead on Mydei’s, refusing to stop looking at Mydei for even the smallest blink of his eyes. He must have looked strange, for Mydei let out a small snort and pinched his cheek.

“You’re not breathing.”

Phainon would go without breathing for the rest of his life if it meant seeing Mydei like this, having Mydei like this. As this thought crossed his mind, however, he realized its futility, and laughed aloud.

“What.” Mydei was staring at him, eyes narrowed.

“Nothing,” Phainon grinned down at him. He finally felt like he could breathe freely again, after days of struggling to stay above water.

“I just didn’t…”

Mydei was still looking at him, listening.

“Yesterday, I—the blessing, it…made me lose control. When that happened—” Phainon rushed to finish his thought before Mydei could jump to conclusions. “it was not the way I would have approached it.”

“...Approached it?”

Phainon struggled to put his thoughts into words. “Approached…you. In that way. I am not a man inclined to the art of seduction, if you haven’t noticed.”

Mydei’s eyebrow rose a hair.

“I hadn’t noticed.”

“In any case, I would have… Courted you first,” Phainon mumbled, slightly embarrassed.

Mydei was silent for a moment.

“I was. In control.”

Phainon stared at him.

“What?”

“The blessing. I’d felt it before. The first time, it made me lose control on the battlefield. I had to be held back by my father’s men before I tore out my companions’ throats.”

Mydei’s throat bobbed.

“I’ve been blessed by Strife before, and each time it became easier to manage the effects and regain control. So—”

“So yesterday, you…” Phainon’s voice came out as practically a whisper.

Mydei’s eyes were steadfast as he looked straight at Phainon.

“Yesterday was not because I lost myself to Strife.”

Phainon’s chest surged with emotion. Mydei had held Phainon willingly, had kissed him and lain with him of his own free will.

“I thought that you had somehow figured out what I thought of you, and felt the same, so—”

Phainon leaned forward and nipped at Mydei’s jaw, causing the other to suck in a breath. Encouraged, Phainon moved downward, lips finding the hollow between Mydei’s neck and chest.

“Phainon,” Mydei gasped.

“Mydeimos,” Phainon whispered as he felt Mydei’s shiver reverberate through his skin. “Mydei, Mydei,” he repeated as he placed open-mouthed kisses upon Mydei’s neck, mind awash with the knowledge that Mydei had wanted him, still wanted him.

“I do,” Phainon spoke into Mydei’s skin. “I do feel the same, I—”

He broke off sharply as Mydei’s teeth found his ear.

Breaths ragged, Phainon tried to endure.

“I’ve always—”

Mydei didn’t let him finish, cutting him off by covering his mouth with his hand.

“Quiet.”

Phainon listened, and he did not speak any longer, not even when Mydei took him in his hand, not even when Mydei bit Phainon’s lips and kissed him, stroking him until Phainon came with a shout.

He did not speak any longer, not even after he returned the favor and they had cleaned up, not even when he twined his way around Mydei’s body in his bed.

He did not speak any longer, and instead dreamed of a warrior with hair dyed red.

Nothing changed between Mydei and Phainon in the coming days. At least, not much. They still sparred together every morning, then went through the day separate from each other aside from the mandatory shared hour for lunch.

Nothing had changed, and yet everything had.

Phainon had never…had anyone the way he had Mydei now. He’d had infatuations in his youth, small, fluttery things that made his heart race. But he’d never had the courage to act on his feelings, never felt he had the right to indulge in frivolous courtships. Bit by bit, his feelings would eventually drip away, like a leak that had never been fixed.

But this time was different.

Even though Phainon had only recently confronted the depth of his feelings towards Mydei, he still naturally expected them to fade away over time. After all, none of his previous feelings lasted longer than a few short weeks, so why would this time be any different?

Phainon was waiting for the moment when his affection for Mydei would eventually fade, the moment when his chest wouldn’t threaten to strangle his breath at the sight of Mydei’s face.

So far, Phainon was still waiting for that moment to come.

In the meantime, however, he felt content.

A warm feeling surrounded Phainon whenever he walked beside Mydeimos. When Mydei began inviting him over for dinner, offering to cook for him—since when was Mydeimos domestic—Phainon felt a funny tingling in his chest.

Whenever Mydei would look at him a little too long, or when Phainon felt the urge to brush the other’s hair from his face, whenever Mydei would let Phainon touch him like that…

Phainon’s chest—no, his heart—felt full.

At every moment of the day, Phainon could barely restrain himself from touching Mydeimos, from pushing him against the closest wall and kissing him. There was not a moment he did not long to clasp Mydei’s face between his hands, to link his fingers with Phainon’s own.

Phainon ached, and yet he restrained himself.

When Phainon’s control slipped, when his resolve would inevitably crack, Mydei would welcome it, pulling Phainon closer to him, fingers digging into Phainon’s skin as if he was just as desperate as Phainon. That was impossible—there was no way Mydeimos would want him as deeply as Phainon wanted him—but in moments like this, Phainon couldn’t help but wonder what if, what if.

What if…Mydeimos truly…?

Some nights, Mydei would arrive at Phainon’s apartments with a low knock on his door. Phainon would cook—“making salads does not count as cooking, Deliverer,” came Mydeimos’ inevitable, exasperated critique—and make honeyed tea.

When they lay beside each other, everything Phainon tried to repress came out in the form of little touches—brushes to Mydeimos’ face, caresses to the crimson tips of his hair, a finger linked around the other’s pinky, like a promise made by a child.

Mydei was not as liberal as Phainon in his touches, but they still made Phainon feel…safe. Warm.

When Mydei pulled him closer at night, or even when he would simply brush his knuckles against his in the light of day, Phainon felt unbelievably, irrevocably happy.

Phainon had not known what it felt like to be truly happy for a while, but now he felt like he was drowning in the feeling. If it was possible for him to die of happiness, he was surely on that path, because there was no way this warmth, this peace, was sustainable.

Nothing lasted forever, every good thing Phainon had ever come across had eventually faded away, so this surely would do the same. The more time that passed, however, the less Phainon was sure of this fact.

Unsurprisingly, the change in Phainon’s demeanor was immediately noticed by Castorice.

“Something’s different,” she noted over dinner in the market one day.

Phainon frowned. “Different how?”

“You seem…lighter.”

Phainon did not know what to say to this. He certainly felt lighter, but there was nothing he could particularly point to as the source of the change. Except—

“Did you finally confess?”

Phainon sputtered, almost choking on air until he finally caught his breath, squawking, “You —I—what?”

Castorice hummed into her drink, amused. “To Mydeimos.”

Phainon was taken aback. Castorice was not the first to pick up on the change between the two of them. The day before, Aglaea had needed only to glance at him and Mydeimos entering her office together before she let out a small “hmm”, a hint of warmth twinkling in her eyes. After the meeting, she pulled them aside and advised them to be discreet in public so as not to give the Council ammunition against the Chrysos Heirs for being poor role models.

Not that they would do anything like that, and Phainon knew Aglaea was only doing her duty, but his face felt like it was flushed red for the rest of the day, long after Aglaea’s words had left his ears.

He should have expected Aglaea to know right away of their entanglement, being the goddess of Romance, but clearly that was not the only reason, as Castorice had also picked up on the shift. Phainon huffed a little sigh.

“How did you even know?”

She scoffed. “It’s not like you were subtle, Phainon. You’ve done nothing but fawn over him since he arrived in Okhema.”

Had he? Phainon knew he had been eager for Mydei’s friendship in the beginning, but he had never fawned over him. His displeasure with Castorice’s assessment must have shown on his face, for she giggled and set her cup down on the table.

“Dearest Phainon, didn’t you know you’ve been obsessed with Mydeimos for ages now?”

Phainon flushed. Obsessed? He would never act in such an undignified manner.

“No, I—just wanted to be his friend…” Phainon started to protest, but then trailed off, his mind wandering.

Had he truly only wanted to be Mydeimos’ friend back then?

He shook that thought off. “In any case,” he declared, “I…uh, did. Confess,” he said, the last few words spoken in a mumble to Castorice’s growing amusement.

“Ha!” she cried, eyes bright in triumph.

She was uncharacteristically eager to hear the details of their courtship, most of which Phainon refused to divulge. There was nothing wrong with him and Mydeimos being together, but he selfishly wanted to keep all the precious moments that belonged only to them to himself. Castorice kept prodding, however, no matter how tightly Phainon sealed his lips. Unfortunately, he suspected this would not be the last interrogation he would be subjected to from her.

Time kept passing like this, and Phainon was happy.

By the time Phainon’s birthday arrived in the third month, spring had slowly ambled into Okhema, the peach blossoms blooming into delicate shades of pink. Spring had come, and Phainon’s feelings had not diminished in the slightest. If anything, they had gotten stronger.

Phainon had never known his heart could beat as fast as it did when he gazed upon Mydei’s sleeping face, or how it trembled when Mydei kissed his lips, his jaw, his fingertips. The depths of his affection felt bottomless, and he felt dazed by it, by Mydeimos’ constant, reassuring presence.

There was so much he struggled to say, but he tried. Phainon kissed his devotion into Mydei’s lips, carved his need for Mydei into his skin as he entered him. Since his own arrival in this holy city, Phainon had long cultivated a celebrated career as an orator, but before Mydei he could not speak a single honeyed word. He had not the words to speak his feelings to the other, and could only show him through action.

Until he drew his last breath, Phainon would endeavor to show Mydei just how much he needed his presence.
